stem: A user updates their profile photo, gets a 200 back, then immediately reloads the page and sees the old photo. Which consistency guarantee was violated?

options.text: Linearizability
options.why: Linearizability was indeed violated, but it is the strongest guarantee and names far more than this symptom. Reaching for it here is the common mistake of describing a specific anomaly with the broadest possible term, which tells your team nothing about what to actually fix.

options.text: Read-your-writes consistency
options.why: This is exactly the session guarantee that a client always sees its own prior writes. It is the precise name for this symptom and it points directly at the fix: route the session to the leader, or pin it to a replica known to have caught up.

options.text: Monotonic reads
options.why: Monotonic reads prevents time appearing to go backwards across successive reads — seeing new data, then old data. Here the user never saw the new photo at all, so the anomaly is about their own write, not about ordering between two reads.

options.text: Causal consistency
options.why: Causal consistency concerns operations related by happens-before across different clients, such as seeing a reply before the message it answers. A client failing to observe its own write is the narrower session-level case, not the general causal one.

explanation: This is the classic read-after-write anomaly on a leader-follower setup: the write lands on the leader, the subsequent read is load-balanced to a follower that has not yet applied it. Naming it correctly matters because each session guarantee has a different fix. Read-your-writes is repaired by routing reads for a recently-writing session to the leader for a short window, or by passing the write's log position back to the client and requiring any serving replica to have reached it. Monotonic reads is repaired by pinning a session to one replica. Causal consistency needs dependency tracking across clients. Reaching for 'linearizability' every time you see a staleness bug conflates all three and usually leads to an overcorrection — someone routes all reads to the leader and you trade a UI glitch for a capacity ceiling.
keyTakeaway: Seeing your own write vanish is read-your-writes, not general staleness — the precise name picks the fix.

stem: A colleague says 'we chose AP, so we accept eventual consistency.' What is the most important correction to make?

options.text: CAP's choice only applies while a network partition is actually happening; the interesting tradeoff the rest of the time is latency versus consistency
options.why: This is PACELC's contribution: else, latency or consistency. Partitions are rare, so nearly all of a system's observable consistency behaviour is decided by the latency tradeoff, not by CAP's partition-time choice.

options.text: AP systems can still be strongly consistent if they use quorum reads and writes
options.why: Quorum overlap gives you a strong read in the absence of a partition, but during a partition a minority side either blocks (choosing C) or serves stale data (choosing A). This restates the tradeoff rather than dissolving it.

options.text: CAP's 'availability' means every non-failing node responds, which is stricter than an SLA-level notion of available
options.why: True and worth knowing — CAP availability is an absolute formal property, not '99.9% uptime'. But it is a precision point about definitions rather than the correction that changes how the team designs the system day to day.

options.text: You cannot choose CP or AP globally; it is a per-operation decision
options.why: Also true and useful — a single service often wants linearizable writes and stale-tolerant reads. But it is downstream of the bigger error, which is treating CAP as a description of steady-state behaviour at all.

explanation: CAP is a statement about behaviour during a partition, and partitions are rare. Yet teams routinely quote it to explain everyday staleness, which is a category error: if there is no partition, CAP permits both consistency and availability, and whatever staleness you observe is a choice someone made for latency. PACELC completes the sentence — if Partition, then A or C; Else, L or C. That 'else' branch governs almost all of your system's real behaviour, and it is where the design work actually lives: how many replicas must acknowledge a write, whether reads may be served locally, how much replication lag you will tolerate to save a cross-region round trip. The per-operation point is also correct and worth internalising, but the partition-time framing is the correction that reframes the whole conversation.
keyTakeaway: CAP only speaks during a partition. The rest of the time — which is nearly always — the real tradeoff is latency versus consistency.

references.label: Abadi, 'Consistency Tradeoffs in Modern Distributed Database System Design'

stem: A downstream service has a brief 3-second blip. Your service, which calls it, then stays saturated for 20 minutes after the downstream fully recovers. Client retries are configured with exponential backoff. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The backoff lacks jitter, so retries are synchronised into waves that keep re-saturating the recovering service
options.why: Exponential backoff without randomisation preserves the correlation created by the original outage: every caller that failed at t=0 retries at the same doubled offsets, producing sharp synchronised spikes that repeatedly knock over a service trying to come back.

options.text: The retry budget is too low, so failed requests are being dropped and re-submitted by users
options.why: A low retry budget would reduce load on the downstream, not sustain it. This inverts the direction of the effect — insufficient retrying causes user-visible errors, not a 20-minute self-inflicted saturation.

options.text: The connection pool is undersized, so recovered capacity cannot be used
options.why: An undersized pool would have throttled throughput before the incident too, and would show as queueing on the client with an idle downstream. The stem describes sustained saturation, which means work is arriving, not being blocked at the client.

options.text: The downstream's caches were cold after the blip, so it is slower until they refill
options.why: Cold caches are a real post-incident effect and do extend recovery, but they would produce elevated latency that decays smoothly. They do not explain saturation persisting far beyond the cache fill, nor the characteristic multi-minute overhang.

explanation: This is a retry storm, and the giveaway is the recovery time being an order of magnitude longer than the fault. An outage is a synchronising event: it fails every in-flight request at the same instant. Plain exponential backoff then schedules all of those retries at the same offsets — 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s — so the recovering service is hit by a series of sharp, correlated waves rather than a smooth ramp. Each wave can push it back over its limit, failing another cohort and restarting the cycle. The fix is full jitter: sleep a random duration between zero and the current exponential ceiling, which spreads a cohort into a flat arrival rate. Backoff alone controls the average rate; only jitter breaks the correlation. Pair it with a retry budget capping retries as a fraction of total requests, and a circuit breaker so callers stop entirely when the downstream is clearly down.
keyTakeaway: Backoff sets the rate; jitter breaks the correlation. Without jitter, an outage schedules its own next outage.

references.label: AWS Architecture Blog, 'Exponential Backoff and Jitter'

stem: This handler is meant to make payment creation safe to retry. What breaks in production?

options.text: Two concurrent requests with the same key both pass the SELECT and both charge the customer
options.why: The check and the insert are not atomic, so the window between them is a textbook race. Under retries — which arrive concurrently by construction — two callers read 'no row', both call the PSP, and the customer is charged twice. Only a unique constraint claimed before the side effect closes it.

options.text: The idempotency key is not scoped to the account, so two accounts could collide
options.why: A real hardening step, and worth doing to stop a client's key namespace bleeding across tenants. But keys are normally client-generated UUIDs, so collision is not the failure this code will actually exhibit, and it is not what the retry path exposes.

options.text: The stored record does not include a status, so failed charges look identical to successful ones
options.why: Genuinely missing and it will hurt during reconciliation, since you cannot distinguish 'never charged' from 'charged and failed'. But it is a modelling gap that shows up in operations, not the correctness bug that duplicates a customer's money.

options.text: The external charge happens before the insert, so a crash in between loses the PSP reference
options.why: This is a real second bug — crash after charge, before insert, and the retry charges again. Correct as far as it goes, but it needs a crash to trigger, whereas the check-then-insert race needs only two concurrent retries, which is the normal case.

explanation: Check-then-act is not idempotency; it is a race with extra steps. The fix is to make the database enforce uniqueness and to claim the key *before* the side effect. Insert a row with the idempotency key under a unique constraint in status 'pending' first. If the insert raises a uniqueness violation, another request owns this key: either return its stored result or, if still pending, return 409 and let the client retry. Only after winning the claim do you call the PSP, then update the row to 'succeeded' with the reference. Pass the same key to the PSP so their side deduplicates too — that closes the crash window, because the retry reaches the provider's own dedupe. The general shape is: uniqueness enforced by a constraint, claim before effect, and idempotency keys threaded all the way down the call chain rather than terminating at your boundary.
keyTakeaway: Idempotency comes from a unique constraint claimed before the side effect, never from SELECT-then-INSERT.

stem: You need mutual exclusion for a job that writes to S3, at roughly 200 jobs/minute across 30 workers. A Redis-based lock with a 30s TTL is proposed. Correctness of the S3 write matters — a double-write corrupts customer data. What is the strongest objection?

options.text: A worker can be paused past its TTL, lose the lock, and still complete its write — so you need fencing tokens the storage layer enforces
options.why: This is the fundamental gap. A GC pause, a hypervisor stall, or a slow syscall can suspend a worker past the TTL; the lock service correctly hands the lock to someone else, but the first worker has no idea and its write is still in flight. Only a monotonically increasing token that the storage layer rejects when stale actually prevents the double-write.

options.text: Redis replication is asynchronous, so a failover can hand the same lock to two workers
options.why: A real and well-known weakness — a lock acknowledged by the primary can vanish on failover to a replica that never saw it. But it needs a failover to trigger, while the pause problem happens on a healthy cluster on any ordinary Tuesday, and no amount of consensus in the lock service fixes it.

options.text: 200 jobs/minute will not scale on a single Redis instance
options.why: 200/minute is about 3 operations per second, which is nothing for Redis — it handles six orders of magnitude more. Reaching for a throughput objection here misreads the numbers in the stem and distracts from the correctness question that was actually asked.

options.text: The 30s TTL is too short and should be extended with a heartbeat while work is in progress
options.why: Lease extension reduces how often the race fires but cannot remove it: the process can be paused between the last successful heartbeat and the write, exactly as before. It makes the bug rarer and therefore harder to find, which is arguably worse.

explanation: This is Kleppmann's fencing argument, and it is the thing that separates locks used for efficiency from locks used for correctness. If the lock exists to stop duplicated *work* — don't send the newsletter twice, don't recompute an expensive report — a TTL lock is fine, because the worst case is wasted effort. If the lock exists for *correctness*, a TTL lock cannot deliver it, no matter how good the lock service is. The reason is that the lock holder and the resource are different machines, and nothing stops a stalled holder from waking up and acting on a lease it no longer owns. The fix is a fencing token: the lock service issues a monotonically increasing number with each grant, the worker passes it to the resource, and the resource refuses any token lower than the highest it has seen. The resource must participate — which is exactly why S3 makes this hard, and why the honest answer is often to redesign for idempotency or conditional writes (preconditions, compare-and-swap on an object version) instead of reaching for a lock at all.
keyTakeaway: A lock for efficiency can use a TTL. A lock for correctness needs a fencing token the resource itself enforces.

stem: A leaderless store has N=5 replicas, W=2, R=2. What is the practical consequence?

options.text: Reads may return stale data, because the read and write quorums are not guaranteed to overlap
options.why: Overlap requires R + W > N. Here 2 + 2 = 4, which is not greater than 5, so a read can hit two replicas that both missed the most recent write and return older data with full confidence.

options.text: Writes will fail whenever more than three replicas are unavailable
options.why: Arithmetically true — W=2 needs two live replicas, so four failures block writes — but that is just restating the availability threshold. It says nothing about the correctness property the configuration actually sacrifices.

options.text: The system is strongly consistent but has poor write availability
options.why: Exactly backwards. Low W and low R give excellent availability on both paths and weak consistency. Strong consistency here would need R+W>N, which costs availability, not the other way round.

options.text: Read repair will keep replicas converged, so staleness is not observable
options.why: Read repair fixes divergence it happens to notice, asynchronously and after the fact. It converges replicas over time but does nothing to stop the stale value being returned to the client on the read that triggered it.

explanation: R + W > N is the overlap condition: it guarantees any read quorum shares at least one replica with the latest write quorum, so a correct value is always present in the set you read. With N=5, W=2, R=2 you have no such guarantee, and a read can legitimately miss a recent write entirely. This is not a bug, it is a deliberate position on the latency-versus-consistency axis — low W and low R are cheap and highly available, which is right for metrics, feeds, or caches. The point is to know which one you have chosen. Note also that even with R+W>N, quorums give you a per-key freshness guarantee, not linearizability: concurrent writes, sloppy quorums with hinted handoff, and the absence of a total order across keys all mean you can still observe anomalies. Quorum overlap answers 'will I see the last write to this key', not 'does this system behave like a single machine'.
keyTakeaway: R + W > N buys quorum overlap and nothing more — it is per-key freshness, not linearizability.

stem: Your team wants an odd number of Raft nodes and asks whether to run 3 or 5. What does moving from 3 to 5 actually buy and cost?

options.text: Tolerates 2 failures instead of 1, at the cost of higher write latency because a larger quorum must acknowledge
options.why: Fault tolerance is floor(N/2), so 3 tolerates 1 and 5 tolerates 2. The cost is that commit latency is set by the slowest member of the majority — the 3rd fastest of 5 rather than the 2nd fastest of 3 — which is usually worse, especially across zones.

options.text: Doubles read throughput, because reads can be served from more followers
options.why: Follower reads are a separate feature and are stale unless you use read-index or lease reads. Adding voters does not by itself increase read capacity, and conflating voting members with read replicas is a common and expensive confusion.

options.text: Reduces write latency, because more nodes can acknowledge in parallel
options.why: Parallel dispatch does not help when you must wait for a majority: the quorum size grows from 2 to 3, so you wait on a slower order statistic. More acknowledgers means the required one arrives later, not sooner.

options.text: Eliminates split brain, which is still possible with 3 nodes
options.why: Raft prevents split brain at any size through majority quorums and term numbers — a 3-node cluster cannot elect two leaders in the same term either. This confuses the number of tolerated failures with the safety property itself.

explanation: Raft's safety comes from majority quorums, and the tolerance is floor(N/2): 3 nodes survive 1 loss, 5 survive 2, 7 survive 3. Every step up buys one more simultaneous failure and costs write latency, because a commit waits for the majority to acknowledge and the majority is bounded by its slowest member. Going from 3 to 5 means waiting for the third-fastest instead of the second-fastest, which matters a lot when members sit in different availability zones. Five is the usual choice for a control plane where losing quorum is catastrophic and write volume is low; three is right for most everything else. Beyond 5 you are almost always wrong — 7 nodes buys a third failure you will never see while paying latency on every write. If you need more read capacity, add non-voting learners rather than voters: they replicate the log without joining the quorum, so they cost nothing on the write path.
keyTakeaway: Cluster size buys failure tolerance and costs write latency. Add learners, not voters, when you need read capacity.

references.label: Ongaro & Ousterhout, 'In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm'

stem: A read-heavy service caches results with a 5-minute TTL. Every 5 minutes, database CPU spikes to 100% for about 8 seconds and p99 latency jumps 40x. Hit rate is 97%. What is happening?

options.text: Cache stampede — many keys were populated at the same moment, so they expire together and every miss hits the database simultaneously
options.why: The periodicity matching the TTL exactly is the signature. Keys populated together expire together, and a 3% miss rate concentrated into one instant is a far larger burst than the same misses spread over five minutes.

options.text: The cache is evicting under memory pressure every 5 minutes
options.why: Eviction is driven by memory pressure and write rate, which do not naturally align to a clean 5-minute period. The precise match to the configured TTL points at expiry, not capacity.

options.text: A 97% hit rate is too low; the working set does not fit in cache
options.why: 97% is a healthy hit rate and, spread evenly, 3% misses would be unremarkable. The problem is not the volume of misses but their distribution in time — averages hide the burst entirely.

options.text: Connection pool exhaustion between the service and the database
options.why: Pool exhaustion is a plausible amplifier once the burst starts, but it is a symptom of the stampede rather than its cause. Enlarging the pool would forward more concurrent load to an already-saturated database.

explanation: Two things convert a healthy hit rate into a periodic outage. The first is synchronised expiry: a deploy, a cold start, or a bulk warm populates thousands of keys within the same second, so they all expire within the same second five minutes later. The second is dogpiling: when one hot key expires, every concurrent request for it misses and independently recomputes the same value, so a single expiry produces hundreds of identical database queries. Fix both. For synchronisation, add jitter to the TTL — a random 10-20% spread turns a spike into a plateau. For dogpiling, use request coalescing (singleflight) so only the first miss computes and the rest wait on that result, or serve the stale value while refreshing in the background so no request ever waits on a cold recompute. Probabilistic early expiry, where a key's refresh chance rises as it nears its TTL, achieves much the same thing with less machinery. The general lesson: a mean hit rate tells you nothing about the arrival pattern of misses, and it is the pattern that takes down the database.
keyTakeaway: Jitter your TTLs and coalesce concurrent misses. A 97% hit rate can still be an outage if the 3% arrives all at once.

references.label: Vattani et al., 'Optimal Probabilistic Cache Stampede Prevention'

stem: An order service must write an order row and publish an `OrderPlaced` event, at 500 orders/second. Losing an event means the warehouse never ships. The team proposes writing to Postgres, then publishing to Kafka in the same function. What should you push for?

options.text: The transactional outbox — write the event to a table in the same transaction as the order, and relay it to Kafka separately
options.why: It reduces the dual-write problem to a single local transaction, which the database already makes atomic. The relay may publish a duplicate after a crash, but it can never lose an event, and duplicates are handled by an idempotent consumer.

options.text: Two-phase commit across Postgres and Kafka
options.why: 2PC is blocking: if the coordinator dies between prepare and commit, participants hold locks until it returns. At 500 writes/second that is an availability disaster, and Kafka is not a well-behaved XA participant anyway.

options.text: Publish to Kafka first, then write to Postgres, so the event is never lost
options.why: This trades a lost event for a phantom one: the event is published, the database write fails, and the warehouse ships an order that does not exist. Reordering a dual write moves the failure mode, it does not remove it.

options.text: Keep the dual write but add a retry loop around the Kafka publish
options.why: Retries help with transient broker errors but do nothing for the case that matters — the process dying after the commit and before the publish. The event is gone and no retry loop is alive to notice.

explanation: This is the dual-write problem: two systems, no shared transaction, and any interleaving of failures loses or invents data. The outbox pattern sidesteps it by making the write atomic where atomicity is free. In the same transaction that inserts the order, insert a row into an `outbox` table. A separate relay — a poller, or better, change data capture reading the WAL via Debezium — reads unpublished rows and pushes them to Kafka, marking them sent. If the relay crashes after publishing but before marking, it republishes on restart. That is the deliberate trade: you accept at-least-once delivery and make consumers idempotent, in exchange for never losing an event. This is almost always the right trade, because deduplicating on a business key is easy and reconstructing a lost order is not. The general principle worth carrying: you cannot get atomicity across two systems, so pick which of duplication or loss you can tolerate, and engineer for it explicitly rather than discovering it in an incident.
keyTakeaway: You cannot make two systems atomic. Reduce it to one local transaction, accept duplicates, and make consumers idempotent.

stem: This last-write-wins merge runs on every node of a multi-region store. What is the flaw?

options.text: Wall clocks on different nodes disagree, so a write that genuinely happened later can be silently discarded
options.why: NTP-synced clocks routinely drift tens of milliseconds and can jump backwards on correction. A node with a fast clock stamps a future time and its record wins forever, discarding every genuinely later write from a node whose clock is behind.

options.text: Ties are resolved arbitrarily because `After` returns false for equal timestamps
options.why: A real gap — equal timestamps mean the local record always wins, so different nodes can converge differently, and you need a deterministic tiebreak like node ID. But it is a narrow edge case beside the systematic error that clock skew introduces.

options.text: `time.Now()` includes a monotonic reading in Go, which is meaningless across machines
options.why: Correct about Go's internals — the monotonic component is stripped on marshalling and only used for same-process comparisons — but this is an implementation detail. The design would be broken with any wall-clock source.

options.text: The function does not merge fields, so concurrent edits to different fields lose one side's change
options.why: True, and per-field merging or a CRDT would preserve more intent. But this is a limitation of choosing whole-record LWW at all, not the defect that makes the code silently wrong even for single-field updates.

explanation: Last-write-wins on wall clocks is a data-loss mechanism wearing a merge function's clothes. Clocks on different machines are not comparable: NTP keeps them within tens of milliseconds at best, drifts, and can step backwards during correction. A node whose clock runs fast stamps records with times other nodes cannot beat, so its writes win indefinitely and later writes elsewhere vanish with no error anywhere. The write returned 200 and the data is gone — the worst failure shape there is. The options are: use logical clocks that capture causality, so concurrent writes are detected as conflicts rather than ordered by accident — version vectors let you surface a real conflict to the application; use hybrid logical clocks, which keep timestamps close to wall time for readability while preserving happens-before; or use a CRDT whose merge is commutative, associative and idempotent so ordering stops mattering. If you must use LWW, at minimum use a bounded-uncertainty clock like Spanner's TrueTime, deterministically break ties on node ID, and be explicit in the design doc that concurrent writes silently lose data.
keyTakeaway: Wall clocks do not order events across machines. LWW on `time.Now()` loses writes silently and reports success.

stem: Under a traffic surge, a service's throughput collapses to near zero while CPU sits at 60%. Queue depth is enormous and almost every response is a timeout. Adding replicas does not help. What is the mechanism?

options.text: Congestion collapse — the service is spending its capacity on requests whose clients have already timed out
options.why: An unbounded queue means requests wait longer than the client timeout, so by the time work is dequeued nobody is listening. The service does full work per request and delivers zero useful throughput, and more replicas simply add more useless capacity behind the same queue.

options.text: A downstream dependency is saturated and the service is blocked on it
options.why: That would normally show as low CPU with threads parked on I/O, and adding replicas would still increase pressure downstream rather than doing nothing. The stem's unbounded queue and universal timeouts point at the service's own admission behaviour.

options.text: Garbage collection pauses are consuming the remaining CPU headroom
options.why: Heavy GC would push CPU up, not leave it at 60%, and the effect would be latency jitter rather than a total throughput collapse. It is a plausible amplifier once queues are huge, not the mechanism.

options.text: Lock contention is serialising request handling
options.why: Contention would cap throughput at a plateau and typically shows as low CPU with threads blocked on a mutex. It does not explain the runaway queue growth or why horizontal scaling has no effect at all.

explanation: This is the classic queueing death spiral, and the tell is that throughput falls to zero while CPU is nowhere near saturated. Once mean queue wait exceeds the client timeout, every request that reaches a worker is already abandoned: the service performs the work, produces a response, and writes it to a socket nobody is reading. It is doing full work for zero goodput. Horizontal scaling cannot fix it because the queue, not the compute, is the problem — you have simply added capacity behind the same backlog. The fixes are all about admission control rather than capacity. Bound every queue, and shed at the boundary when it is full; a fast 503 preserves capacity for requests that can still be served. Propagate deadlines with each request and check them before starting work, so abandoned requests are dropped rather than executed — cheap and enormously effective. Use LIFO rather than FIFO when overloaded, because the newest request is the most likely to still have a listener. Adaptive concurrency limits (Little's law applied to observed latency, as in Netflix's concurrency-limits) do this automatically. The instinct to correct here is that a full queue is not a buffer to be enlarged; it is a signal to say no.
keyTakeaway: Unbounded queues convert overload into total collapse. Bound the queue, propagate deadlines, and shed early.

references.label: Google SRE Book, ch. 22 'Addressing Cascading Failures'

stem: A vendor claims their queue provides exactly-once delivery. What is the most accurate response?

options.text: Exactly-once delivery is impossible; what is achievable is exactly-once processing, via at-least-once delivery plus idempotent or transactional consumers
options.why: The distinction is the whole point. Delivery cannot be exactly-once because the sender can never distinguish a lost message from a lost acknowledgement, so it must choose to retry or not. Effects can still be applied once, which is what anyone actually wants.

options.text: It is possible within a single broker cluster but not across clusters
options.why: Cluster topology is not the obstacle. The impossibility comes from the acknowledgement being as loseable as the message itself, which is equally true between two processes on one machine as across a WAN.

options.text: It is achievable if the broker persists messages synchronously to disk before acknowledging
options.why: Durable writes stop messages being lost in the broker, which is necessary but unrelated. The ambiguity lives in the network between broker and consumer, and no amount of fsync on the broker resolves it.

options.text: It is achievable with TCP, since TCP already guarantees exactly-once delivery of bytes
options.why: TCP deduplicates within one connection's lifetime and nothing more. When the connection drops mid-stream — the case that matters — the application cannot tell what the peer received, which is exactly the original problem.

explanation: The Two Generals problem is the reason: a sender that gets no acknowledgement cannot distinguish 'message lost' from 'acknowledgement lost', so it either retries (risking a duplicate) or does not (risking a loss). No protocol removes that choice, so exactly-once *delivery* is not available at any price. What is available is exactly-once *processing*: deliver at least once, and make the effect happen once. Three mechanisms do this. Idempotent operations, where applying twice equals applying once — `SET status='shipped'` rather than `counter += 1`. Deduplication on a stored message ID, where the consumer records processed IDs and skips repeats, with the dedupe write in the same transaction as the effect. Or a transactional read-process-write within one system, which is what Kafka's 'exactly-once semantics' actually is — it commits consumer offsets and produced records atomically within Kafka, and explicitly does not extend to your database or a third-party API call. Read every 'exactly-once' claim as scoped to a boundary and go find where that boundary is, because your side effects are usually outside it.
keyTakeaway: Exactly-once delivery is impossible; exactly-once processing is an idempotent consumer. Ask where the vendor's boundary ends.

stem: A multi-tenant analytics system shards by `tenant_id`. Three tenants out of 40,000 generate 60% of all traffic, and their shards are at 95% CPU while others idle at 5%. Resharding requires a maintenance window the business will not grant. What is the best move?

options.text: Split the hot tenants across sub-shards using a composite key, keeping the existing scheme for everyone else
options.why: It targets the actual problem — a handful of keys too large for one shard — without touching the 39,997 tenants that are fine. Only the hot tenants need a fan-out read path, so the complexity is contained where it earns its keep.

options.text: Switch to consistent hashing so keys distribute more evenly
options.why: Consistent hashing minimises reshuffling when nodes change; it does nothing about a single key being too hot. If one tenant exceeds a shard's capacity, every hash function in the world still maps that tenant to exactly one shard.

options.text: Add read replicas for the hot shards
options.why: Worth doing if the load is read-dominated, and it may buy time. But it leaves writes concentrated on the same primary and does not address a hot shard's storage or write ceiling, so it defers the problem rather than fixing it.

options.text: Move the three tenants to dedicated infrastructure
options.why: A legitimate strategy — large customers often end up on their own stack for isolation and billing reasons — but it is an operational and commercial project, not a fix, and it recurs the moment a fourth tenant grows.

explanation: This is the hot-key problem, and the essential insight is that no hashing scheme helps when a single key exceeds one shard's capacity. Hashing distributes keys; it cannot subdivide one. The fix is to give hot keys more key space: shard on `(tenant_id, bucket)` where `bucket` is a small salt derived from something naturally distributed — a timestamp window, a user ID, or a random number in a range sized per tenant. The hot tenant now occupies N shards instead of one. The cost is that reads for that tenant must fan out across its buckets and merge, so keep a small registry of which tenants are split and how many buckets each has, and let everyone else take the simple single-shard path. Two things to carry forward. First, tenant-based sharding always eventually meets a tenant too big for a shard, so design the split mechanism before you need it under pressure. Second, this is why maintenance windows for resharding are a trap: build online resharding — dual-write, backfill, verify, cut over — early, because you will need it at the worst possible moment.
keyTakeaway: Hashing distributes keys but cannot split one. Give hot keys more key space with a composite key, and fan out reads only for them.

stem: One node in a 12-node fleet passes every health check and stays in the load balancer, but requests routed to it are 50x slower and 4% of them fail. Dashboards show the fleet as healthy. What is this called, and what is the underlying problem?

options.text: Gray failure — the node's self-assessment differs from the experience of its clients, and health checks measure the wrong thing
options.why: The defining property is differential observability: the node genuinely believes it is fine because `/health` returns 200, while callers see a degraded dependency. Any detector that asks a component about itself will miss this class of fault entirely.

options.text: A Byzantine fault, since the node reports healthy while behaving incorrectly
options.why: Byzantine faults involve arbitrary or malicious behaviour, including lying about state. This node is honestly reporting the shallow thing it was asked to check — the fault is in the question, not in the answer, and Byzantine machinery would not help.

options.text: A partial network partition between that node and the load balancer
options.why: A partition on that path would make health checks fail too, removing the node from rotation — which is the outcome you want. The stem's whole point is that traffic keeps flowing because the check keeps passing.

options.text: Cascading failure in an early stage
options.why: Cascading failure is load shifting from failed components to survivors until they fall in turn. Here the fleet is stable and one node is quietly degraded, with no propagation — the shape and the remedy are both different.

explanation: Gray failure is where most real production pain lives, and it is defined by differential observability: the system's internal view of its health diverges from what its clients experience. A shallow `/health` that returns 200 if the process is running is nearly useless — it verifies only that a socket is open. The node may have a wedged connection pool, a full disk, a corrupted local cache, a failing NIC dropping 4% of packets, or a noisy neighbour on the hypervisor. Three habits address this. Make health checks deep: exercise the real dependency path, not just the process, so a broken pool shows up as unhealthy. Judge health from the caller's side — per-upstream error rate and latency, with outlier detection that ejects a host whose stats deviate from its peers, which is what Envoy does. And alert on percentiles per host, never fleet aggregates, because one bad node in twelve is invisible in a fleet-wide p99 and glaring in a per-host one. The general instinct: a component asked about itself will tell you what it can see, and the fault you care about is usually in what it cannot.
keyTakeaway: Health checks ask a node about itself. Gray failure is when that answer and the client's experience diverge — measure from the caller.

references.label: Huang et al., 'Gray Failure: The Achilles Heel of Cloud-Scale Systems'

stem: A request fans out to 100 shards and must wait for all of them. Each shard has a p99 of 200ms and a median of 10ms. Measured end-to-end p50 is around 200ms and users complain it feels slow. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Send a hedged second request to another replica if the first has not returned by roughly the 95th percentile
options.why: Hedging directly attacks the order statistic that is hurting you. A small number of duplicate requests — around 5% extra load — collapses the fan-out's dependence on any single slow replica, and Dean and Barroso measured exactly this effect in production.

options.text: Reduce the number of shards so fewer replicas are involved
options.why: It does reduce tail amplification, but shard count is normally set by data size and per-shard capacity. Trading throughput ceiling and storage layout for latency is a much bigger structural concession than hedging, and usually unavailable.

options.text: Optimise the median case, since the median is what most requests experience
options.why: This is the trap the question is built around. With 100 parallel shards the overall latency is the maximum of 100 draws, so it is governed by the tail of the per-shard distribution. Halving a 10ms median changes almost nothing.

options.text: Increase timeouts so slow shards have a chance to complete
options.why: Longer timeouts make the observed latency worse, not better — you wait longer for the same straggler. It also removes the ceiling that keeps a pathological replica from holding a request open indefinitely.

explanation: This is tail-at-scale, and the arithmetic is the point. If a request waits for 100 independent shards, the probability that none of them lands in its p99 is 0.99^100, about 37%. So roughly 63% of your requests contain at least one shard responding at p99 speed, and your end-to-end median is set by your per-shard p99. Fan-out converts other people's tails into your median. This is why optimising the median is wasted effort here and why per-shard p99 is the number to watch. Hedged requests are the standard remedy: wait until the request has taken longer than about 95% normally do, then issue a duplicate to a different replica and take whichever answers first, cancelling the loser. Because only 5% of requests ever hedge, the extra load is small while the latency improvement is large. Related tools: tied requests, where a replica dequeuing the work tells its twin to drop it; micro-partitioning so slow shards can be rebalanced off a struggling host; and returning partial results with a completeness indicator when the product can tolerate it. The habit to build is to reason about which order statistic your architecture actually exposes to the user, then measure that one.
keyTakeaway: Fan-out makes your p50 a function of your components' p99. Hedge requests instead of optimising the median.

stem: Service A calls B, which calls C. Each hop is configured as below. What is wrong?

code.content:
service_a:
  timeout_calling_b: 1s
  retries: 3

service_b:
  timeout_calling_c: 3s
  retries: 3

service_c:
  p99_latency: 800ms

options.text: B's timeout exceeds A's, so B keeps working on requests A has abandoned, and retries multiply into 9x load on C
options.why: A gives up after 1s while B waits up to 3s for C, so B burns capacity on dead requests. Worse, retries compound multiplicatively down the chain: 3 attempts from A times 3 from B is 9 requests hitting C for one user action.

options.text: C's p99 of 800ms is too close to A's 1s timeout, so a normal slow request will time out
options.why: A genuine sizing concern — you want real headroom over the downstream p99 — but it describes the tuning of one number. The structural defect is that the timeouts are not ordered and the retries compound, which no amount of tuning fixes.

options.text: Three retries is too many; one is standard
options.why: Retry count is a judgement call and three is defensible on an idempotent call to a flaky dependency. Stating a fixed correct number misses that the danger here is the product of retries across hops, not the value at any single one.

options.text: The configuration does not specify whether timeouts are per-attempt or total
options.why: An important ambiguity, and per-attempt timeouts with retries do let total time far exceed the nominal budget. But it is a gap in the specification rather than the defect present in the system as written.

explanation: Two rules are broken. First, timeouts must decrease as you go down the call chain: if B's budget for C exceeds A's budget for B, B is guaranteed to spend time on work whose client has left. Every downstream timeout should be strictly less than its caller's remaining budget. Second, retries compound multiplicatively — 3 at A times 3 at B is 9 requests at C for a single user action, and a mild wobble at C becomes a 9x amplification exactly when C can least afford it. The robust fix is deadline propagation rather than per-hop timeouts: A computes an absolute deadline, passes it in metadata (gRPC does this natively), and each hop derives its own budget from the time remaining, checking before starting work and abandoning immediately if it has passed. For retries, pick one layer — usually the edge — to own them, use a retry budget capping retries at a small fraction of total requests rather than a per-request count, and add a circuit breaker so a sustained failure stops the traffic instead of amplifying it. The instinct worth building: whenever you see retries at more than one layer, multiply them and ask whether the bottom of the stack can survive the product.
keyTakeaway: Timeouts must shrink down the call chain and retries multiply along it. Propagate deadlines; retry at one layer, on a budget.

stem: A cache cluster uses `hash(key) % N` to pick a node. What specifically goes wrong when N changes from 10 to 11, and what does consistent hashing fix?

options.text: Almost every key maps to a different node, so nearly the whole cache misses at once; consistent hashing remaps only about 1/N of keys
options.why: Changing the modulus changes the result for roughly (N-1)/N of all keys — about 91% here — so a single node addition empties the cache and stampedes the origin. Consistent hashing places nodes on a ring so only the keys in one arc move.

options.text: Keys distribute unevenly because 11 is prime; consistent hashing uses a better hash function
options.why: Primality of the modulus affects distribution quality only for poor hash functions, and consistent hashing is not about hash quality at all — it is about how many keys have to move when membership changes.

options.text: Hash collisions increase; consistent hashing eliminates them with virtual nodes
options.why: Collisions in the key space are unrelated to the modulus, and virtual nodes exist to smooth load imbalance across the ring, not to remove collisions. Two independent concepts get conflated here.

options.text: The distribution becomes unbalanced; consistent hashing guarantees perfectly even distribution
options.why: Modulo hashing is actually well balanced with a decent hash. Plain consistent hashing is the one with balance problems — arcs come out uneven — which is precisely why virtual nodes were introduced to patch it.

explanation: With `hash(key) % N`, the node for a key depends on N, so changing N reassigns roughly (N-1)/N of the key space. Going from 10 nodes to 11 moves about 91% of keys — every one of them a cache miss, arriving simultaneously, on an origin sized for a 97% hit rate. Consistent hashing puts both nodes and keys on a ring and assigns each key to the next node clockwise. Adding a node only captures the arc between it and its predecessor, so only about 1/N of keys move and the rest stay put. The catch is that randomly placed nodes produce uneven arcs, so real implementations give each physical node many virtual nodes — 100 to 200 points on the ring — which smooths the distribution by averaging. Worth knowing that this is not the only answer: rendezvous hashing (highest random weight) achieves the same minimal-disruption property with less machinery and better balance, and jump consistent hash is faster still when nodes are numbered contiguously. The underlying instinct generalises beyond caches — whenever a placement decision depends on the size of the fleet, membership changes become mass migrations.
keyTakeaway: Modulo hashing makes N part of every key's identity, so scaling invalidates almost everything. Ring or rendezvous hashing moves only 1/N.

references.label: Karger et al., 'Consistent Hashing and Random Trees'

stem: A recommendations service is called on every product page render at 3,000 rps. It occasionally degrades to 5-second latency for several minutes. Product says a page without recommendations is acceptable; a page that fails to load is not. What is the right protection?

options.text: A circuit breaker with a short timeout that falls back to a static list, opening on error or latency rate
options.why: This matches the stated product constraint exactly: recommendations are optional, page loads are not. Breaking the circuit stops threads piling up on a slow dependency, and the fallback keeps the page whole while the dependency recovers unpressured.

options.text: Aggressive retries with backoff, so transient slowness is smoothed over
options.why: Retrying a dependency that is slow rather than failing adds load to something already struggling and multiplies the time the caller waits. Retries suit brief transient errors, not a multi-minute latency degradation.

options.text: A bulkhead limiting the connection pool for this dependency, with no fallback
options.why: The bulkhead is genuinely worth having and belongs alongside the breaker — it stops one dependency consuming all threads. Without a fallback, though, requests that fail to get a slot still break the page, which product has ruled out.

options.text: Increase the timeout to 6 seconds so calls succeed during the degradation
options.why: This propagates the dependency's worst latency straight to the user and holds request-handling capacity for the duration. It converts an optional feature's problem into a whole-site problem — the opposite of what the constraint asks for.

explanation: The load-bearing sentence is the product constraint: recommendations are optional, the page is not. That immediately classifies the dependency as non-critical, and non-critical dependencies should fail fast with a fallback rather than being waited on. A circuit breaker tracks the error and slow-call rate over a rolling window; when it crosses a threshold it opens, and calls return the fallback immediately without touching the network. After a cooldown it goes half-open, letting a trickle through to test recovery, and closes if they succeed. Two design points people get wrong. Trip on latency, not just errors — a dependency at 5 seconds is failing even though every call returns 200, and an errors-only breaker will never open. And set the timeout from the product's latency budget rather than the dependency's p99: if the page must render in 300ms, the timeout is well under that regardless of what the recommender considers normal. Pair the breaker with a bulkhead so this dependency can never consume more than its share of threads or connections, and make sure the fallback path is exercised regularly — untested fallbacks fail exactly when they are needed. The habit worth forming is classifying every dependency as critical or optional at design time, because that single label determines timeout, fallback, and whether it belongs on the request path at all.
keyTakeaway: Classify every dependency as critical or optional first. Optional ones get a short timeout, a breaker that trips on latency, and a tested fallback.

stem: A reporting replica normally lags the primary by under a second. During a nightly bulk import it falls 45 minutes behind, even though the replica's CPU, disk and network are all well under capacity. Why?

options.text: Replication apply is largely single-threaded, so the replica cannot parallelise a write stream the primary produced with many concurrent connections
options.why: The primary accepts writes across dozens of connections in parallel; a replica applying a serial log has far less concurrency available, so its effective write throughput is much lower. Idle resources with growing lag is the signature of a serialisation bottleneck.

options.text: The network link saturates during bulk transfer
options.why: Directly contradicted by the stem, which says network utilisation is low. It is also usually wrong in practice, since logical or physical log records are far smaller than the queries that produced them.

options.text: Long-running report queries hold locks that block replication apply
options.why: A genuine mechanism on some engines — Postgres will pause or cancel replay under conflicting queries depending on `hot_standby_feedback` — but it would normally show as replay conflicts and cancelled queries, which the stem does not mention.

options.text: The replica is fsyncing every transaction while the primary batches them
options.why: Durability settings do affect apply throughput, but this would push disk utilisation up rather than leaving it low. The stem explicitly rules out disk being the constraint.

explanation: The primary and the replica have asymmetric parallelism, and that asymmetry is what bulk writes expose. The primary executes writes across many concurrent client connections; the replica reads a mostly sequential log and, historically, applies it with a single thread. So the replica's ceiling can be a small fraction of the primary's, and a workload that keeps the primary comfortable can put the replica into unbounded lag. Idle CPU, disk and network with growing lag is the tell for a serialisation bottleneck rather than a resource one. Practical responses: enable parallel apply where the engine supports it (MySQL's `replica_parallel_workers` with `WRITESET` dependency tracking, or Postgres's parallel WAL apply in recent versions); throttle bulk imports and chunk them with pauses so the replica keeps up; run imports against a separate path that does not go through the same replication stream; or accept the lag and make it explicit — alert on lag as an SLI, and make consumers of the replica aware of a staleness bound rather than assuming freshness. The broader instinct is that any replication stream has a throughput ceiling independent of the primary's, and you should know what that ceiling is before a bulk job discovers it for you.
keyTakeaway: A replica's apply path is usually far less parallel than the primary's write path. Lag with idle resources means serialisation, not capacity.

stem: A booking flow spans flights, hotels and payment, each owned by a different team with its own database. A saga with compensating transactions is proposed. What is the most important thing to design for, that teams usually miss?

options.text: Compensations are not rollbacks — intermediate states are visible to other actors, so you need semantic undo and a story for what people saw
options.why: A saga has no isolation. A held seat is really held, a charge really settles, and a confirmation email really sends before a later step fails. Compensation must undo the business meaning of that publicly-observed state, which is a product decision, not a database one.

options.text: Every step must be idempotent, since the orchestrator will retry
options.why: Necessary and non-negotiable, but it is the well-known part that teams do build. It makes the saga safe to retry without addressing what the world already saw between the forward step and its compensation.

options.text: Choosing orchestration over choreography, so the flow is traceable
options.why: A sound architectural preference for a flow this size — a central orchestrator makes state and failure handling visible where choreography scatters them. But it concerns how you implement the saga, not the semantic hazard the pattern carries.

options.text: Persisting saga state durably so it survives an orchestrator restart
options.why: Essential mechanics, and a saga without durable state is broken. It is table stakes that any workflow engine provides for free, though, and it does not touch the modelling problem that makes sagas hard.

explanation: A saga trades atomicity and isolation for availability across service boundaries, and it is isolation that teams underestimate. In an ACID transaction, no one sees intermediate state; in a saga, everyone does. The seat is unavailable to other customers, the card is charged, the confirmation is sent — and then the hotel step fails. Compensation cannot rewind reality, it can only apply a new business action: refund the charge, release the seat, send a cancellation. So the design work is semantic. Ask, for each step, what an outside observer can see between forward and compensating action, and whether that is acceptable — this is a product conversation about apology emails and refund timing, not a technical one. Then handle the hard cases explicitly: compensations that themselves fail need retry-forever plus an alert and a manual path, since there is no compensation for a compensation. Watch for actions that cannot be undone at all — a sent email, a dispatched parcel — and order the saga so those come last, after every step that could still fail. Where isolation genuinely matters, use a semantic lock: mark the record `pending` so other flows can see it is in flight and decline to act. And prefer an orchestrator with durable execution (Temporal, Step Functions) over hand-rolled state machines, because the retry, timeout and versioning semantics are where hand-rolled sagas quietly rot.
keyTakeaway: Sagas give up isolation, not just atomicity. Design what the world sees mid-saga, and put irreversible steps last.

stem: A primary-replica database uses an external monitor to promote the replica when the primary stops responding. What must be in place to prevent split brain, and why is a heartbeat timeout insufficient?

options.text: Fencing — the old primary must be forcibly cut off from clients or storage, because an unresponsive primary may still be alive and serving
options.why: Absence of a heartbeat proves nothing about liveness: it could be a network partition, a long GC pause, or an overloaded monitor. Only actively fencing the old primary — STONITH, revoking its storage lease, or pulling its network access — makes the assumption true.

options.text: A longer heartbeat timeout, so transient network blips do not trigger a promotion
options.why: This trades one failure for another: longer timeouts mean longer real outages, and no finite timeout can distinguish a dead node from a slow one. It reduces the frequency of the bug while leaving it fully possible.

options.text: Synchronous replication, so no writes are lost when the replica is promoted
options.why: Synchronous replication addresses data loss at failover, which is a different and also important problem. It does nothing to stop two nodes both believing they are primary and accepting conflicting writes afterwards.

options.text: A third monitor node, so promotion decisions require a majority vote
options.why: Quorum stops the monitors from disagreeing among themselves, which is real progress and worth having. But a correct, unanimous decision to promote still leaves the old primary running and accepting writes unless something fences it.

explanation: The core issue is that failure detection is fundamentally unreliable in an asynchronous network: you cannot distinguish a crashed node from a slow one or an unreachable one. So 'the primary stopped responding' is never evidence that it stopped working. It may be partitioned from the monitor while still perfectly reachable by half your application servers, or paused in GC for eight seconds and about to resume mid-write. Promote the replica in that state and you have two primaries taking conflicting writes, which is unrecoverable without manual reconciliation. Fencing turns the assumption into a fact. The forms it takes: STONITH, where you power off or reboot the old node via out-of-band management; storage-level fencing, revoking its lease or write access on shared storage; network fencing, removing it from the service mesh or load balancer; and fencing tokens, where a monotonically increasing epoch number accompanies every write and the storage layer rejects anything from an older epoch. Quorum-based monitoring and fencing are complements, not alternatives — quorum makes the decision trustworthy, fencing makes it effective. This is also why managed failover in cloud databases takes tens of seconds: most of that time is spent making certain the old primary is really gone.
keyTakeaway: You cannot tell a dead node from a slow one. Promotion is only safe once the old primary has been actively fenced.

stem: A team wants per-user ordering of events in Kafka and configures the producer as below. What breaks?

code.content:
# Producer
partitioner=RoundRobinPartitioner
acks=all
retries=10
max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=5
enable.idempotence=false

# Consumer: 6 instances in one group, 12 partitions

options.text: Round-robin partitioning spreads one user's events across partitions, and Kafka only orders within a partition
options.why: Kafka's ordering guarantee is per-partition, full stop. Round-robin deliberately scatters a user's events across all 12 partitions, which are consumed independently and concurrently, so per-user order is lost before the consumer even starts.

options.text: `max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=5` with retries can reorder messages within a partition
options.why: A real and subtle bug — without idempotence, a retried batch can land after a later one — and worth fixing by enabling idempotence. But it is a secondary reordering risk layered on top of a partitioning choice that has already destroyed ordering outright.

options.text: Six consumers cannot cover 12 partitions, so some events are never processed
options.why: Consumer group assignment gives each of the six consumers two partitions; all 12 are covered. Fewer consumers than partitions is the normal, healthy configuration — the reverse, more consumers than partitions, leaves some idle.

options.text: `acks=all` slows the producer enough that events arrive out of order
options.why: `acks=all` affects durability and latency, not ordering, and is the correct setting when you care about not losing data. Slower acknowledgement does not reorder anything; in-flight count and retries do.

explanation: Kafka guarantees order within a partition and offers nothing across partitions. To get per-user ordering, the user ID must be the partition key, so every event for that user hashes to the same partition and is consumed in sequence by one consumer. Round-robin explicitly opts out of that. Fix the partitioner first, then close the secondary hole: set `enable.idempotence=true`, which pins `acks=all`, bounds in-flight requests appropriately and gives the producer sequence numbers so a retry cannot land out of order or duplicate. Two consequences to plan for once you key by user. Hot keys — a very active user can make one partition the bottleneck, and no rebalancing helps because the key must stay put. And repartitioning changes the key-to-partition mapping, so adding partitions breaks ordering for in-flight keys; treat partition count as close to immutable and size it generously up front. Finally, remember the guarantee is per partition per consumer: if your consumer hands work to a thread pool, you have thrown the ordering away again inside your own process, which is one of the most common ways teams lose it after getting the producer right.
keyTakeaway: Kafka orders within a partition only. Order by key means partition by key — and don't re-parallelise inside the consumer.

stem: You must enforce 1,000 requests/minute per API key across 50 stateless gateway nodes. Occasional small overshoot is acceptable; adding 20ms to every request is not. What design fits?

options.text: Local token buckets holding a share of the budget, periodically reconciled against a shared counter
options.why: The common path stays in memory with no network hop, meeting the latency constraint, while periodic reconciliation keeps the fleet-wide total roughly correct. It trades exactness for latency, which is precisely the trade the stem permits.

options.text: A shared Redis counter incremented on every request with `INCR` and a TTL
options.why: Accurate and simple, but it puts a network round trip on every single request — the cost the stem rules out — and makes Redis a hard dependency on the request path, so its failure becomes an outage or a silent bypass.

options.text: Divide the limit by 50 and enforce 20 requests/minute per node locally
options.why: Fast and stateless, but it breaks under uneven load: a key whose traffic lands mostly on three nodes gets throttled at 60/minute while the fleet-wide budget sits unused. Load balancers do not distribute per-key traffic evenly.

options.text: Sticky routing by API key so each key is always handled by one node, which enforces the limit locally
options.why: It does give exact limits with no shared state, and is a legitimate design. But it couples rate limiting to routing, creates hot nodes for busy keys, and turns every node failure or scaling event into a rebalance of limit state.

explanation: Rate limiting distributed across N nodes is a consistency problem wearing a different hat, and the stem hands you the answer by naming the tolerances: small overshoot fine, per-request latency not. That rules out any design with a synchronous round trip and rules in an approximate one. The standard shape is a local token bucket per node holding a slice of the global budget, refilled from a shared store on a timer — say every second — rather than per request. Nodes that are consuming quickly claim a larger share on the next reconcile; idle nodes give theirs back. Overshoot is bounded by roughly the reconcile interval times the fleet's aggregate rate, so you can compute the worst case rather than hope. Two refinements worth knowing. Make the reconcile adaptive: a node near the end of its allocation should refresh sooner, which keeps overshoot low when it matters and chatter low when it does not. And fail open or closed deliberately — decide up front what happens when the shared store is unreachable, because the default is usually 'unlimited' and nobody notices until an incident. Sliding-window counters give smoother enforcement than fixed windows, which allow a 2x burst across a window boundary. The transferable idea is that 'exact' is a requirement to be negotiated, and naming your tolerance for error is what unlocks the cheap design.
keyTakeaway: Ask what overshoot you can tolerate before designing a limiter. A stated error budget buys you a local, in-memory fast path.

references.label: Stripe, 'Scaling your API with rate limiters'

stem: After a routine deploy that restarts all 40 pods within about 15 seconds, the service takes four minutes to become healthy and the database sees 10x its normal connection count. Steady-state load is unremarkable. What is the mechanism?

options.text: Synchronised cold start — every pod initialises connection pools, warms caches and reloads config simultaneously, so startup cost arrives as one spike
options.why: Restarting a fleet together correlates every pod's startup work into the same 15-second window. Connection pool pre-warming alone multiplies by 40, and the database sees a burst that has nothing to do with steady-state traffic.

options.text: Connection leaks from the previous pods that have not yet timed out
options.why: Lingering connections from terminated pods do add pressure, but they drain on TCP timeouts rather than causing a 10x spike, and graceful shutdown normally closes them. It would also not explain the four-minute recovery.

options.text: The readiness probe is misconfigured, so pods take traffic before they are ready
options.why: This would cause errors on early requests rather than a database connection storm, and it does not explain the correlation with deploy timing. A plausible contributor to the symptoms, not the cause of the spike.

options.text: The database is undersized for the fleet's steady-state connection count
options.why: Explicitly contradicted by the stem, which says steady-state load is unremarkable. If the fleet's normal connection count were the issue, the problem would persist rather than resolving after four minutes.

explanation: This is the thundering herd applied to deploys, and it is the same underlying pathology as retry storms and cache stampedes: an event that correlates work which is normally spread out. Forty pods each opening a pre-warmed pool of, say, 20 connections is 800 connections arriving in seconds, plus 40 simultaneous config fetches, 40 cache warms, and 40 service-discovery registrations. Each is fine alone and lethal together. The fixes are all about decorrelation and pacing. Roll deploys gradually with a `maxSurge`/`maxUnavailable` that keeps the replacement rate low, rather than replacing the fleet at once. Add randomised startup jitter, a few seconds per pod, so initialisation spreads out. Size connection pools by minimum rather than pre-warming to maximum, and let them grow under real demand. Put a connection pooler such as PgBouncer in front of the database so pod count and database connection count decouple entirely — this is the structural fix and usually the right one. And check that startup work is actually needed at boot: cache warming is often better done lazily with a singleflight guard than eagerly by every instance. The habit to build is scanning any design for events that synchronise otherwise-independent work, because that is where capacity plans quietly fail.
keyTakeaway: Deploys, restarts and outages all correlate work that is normally spread out. Jitter the startup and pool the connections.

stem: A product with users in the US and EU wants sub-100ms writes in both regions and a single logical dataset. Cross-region round trip is 90ms. Leadership asks for active-active. What must you tell them?

options.text: Synchronous cross-region consensus cannot meet a 100ms write budget, so they must choose per-dataset: partition by region, accept async replication with conflicts, or relax the latency target
options.why: A single 90ms round trip consumes almost the entire budget before any work happens, and quorum needs at least one. Naming the three real options turns an impossible request into a decision leadership can actually make.

options.text: Active-active is achievable with CRDTs, which resolve conflicts automatically without coordination
options.why: CRDTs do give coordination-free convergence and are the right tool for some data. But they only support operations with the right algebraic structure — you cannot express 'reserve the last seat' or a uniqueness constraint — so they solve a subset, not the general case.

options.text: Use a global database like Spanner, which provides strong consistency across regions
options.why: Spanner does give external consistency globally, but not for free: cross-region writes still pay consensus latency, typically well over 100ms. It changes who implements the tradeoff, not whether physics allows it.

options.text: Route all writes to a single primary region and accept higher latency for the other
options.why: A perfectly reasonable design and often the right one — it is simple and strongly consistent. But it is one of the options rather than the answer, and presenting it alone concedes the latency target without exploring partitioning, which may satisfy everyone.

explanation: The senior move here is to convert an impossible requirement into an explicit choice, using the numbers. A 90ms cross-region round trip means any write requiring agreement from both regions costs at least 90ms of pure network before execution, so sub-100ms global consensus is off the table regardless of vendor. Present three real options and let the business pick per dataset. Partition by region: each user's data is homed where they are, writes are local and fast, and cross-region access is rare and slow. This is the best answer for most consumer products and it is what data residency rules often push you toward anyway. Asynchronous multi-master: both regions accept writes locally and replicate in the background, which means real conflicts you must resolve with CRDTs where the semantics allow, or application-level merge rules where they do not. Or relax the target: writes go to one region at around 100-150ms for the far side while reads stay local and fast, which is frequently invisible to users because reads dominate. Crucially this is a per-dataset decision — a user's profile can be regionally homed while a global inventory count needs coordination and a feature flag can be eventually consistent. The reason this question separates senior from staff is that the answer is not a technology but a facilitated tradeoff, delivered with the latency arithmetic that makes the constraint undeniable.
keyTakeaway: The speed of light is a requirement, not a bug. Turn 'we want active-active' into a per-dataset choice between partitioning, conflicts, and latency.

references.label: Corbett et al., 'Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database'

stem: You are 25 minutes into an incident. Checkout is failing for roughly 30% of users, you suspect a bad deploy but have not confirmed it, and a rollback is in progress with an ETA of 10 minutes. Which status update should you post to the company-wide channel?

options.text: "Checkout failing for ~30% of users since 14:05. Suspected cause: the 13:52 deploy — not yet confirmed. Rollback in progress, ETA 14:40. Next update at 14:40 or sooner if this changes. I'm IC; @sara is comms."
options.why: It leads with customer impact and its start time, separates the confirmed from the suspected, gives a concrete next-update commitment, and names roles so people know who to ask. That combination is what stops a channel filling with speculation and side-questions.

options.text: "Investigating elevated error rates in the checkout service. Will update when we know more."
options.why: Too vague to act on: no impact figure, no time bound, and 'when we know more' guarantees a stream of people asking for updates. It is technically accurate and operationally useless, which is the most common failure mode of incident comms.

options.text: "The 13:52 deploy broke checkout. Rolling back now, should be fixed in 10 minutes. Sorry all."
options.why: States an unconfirmed cause as fact. If the rollback does not fix it you have burned credibility and sent everyone down the wrong path, and the apology consumes space that impact and next-update timing should occupy.

options.text: "p99 latency on checkout-api is elevated and we're seeing 500s from the payment adapter. Looking at the deploy diff and the PSP dashboard. Thread below for details."
options.why: This is the engineering-channel update written for the wrong audience. It describes symptoms in internal terms without telling a company-wide reader how many customers are affected or when they will hear next.

explanation: Incident communication is a distinct skill from incident debugging, and it is one of the clearest senior signals available, because it is visible to everyone. A good update has four elements. Impact in customer terms with a number and a start time — '30% of checkouts since 14:05', not 'elevated error rates'. A clear separation of what is confirmed from what is suspected, because stating an unconfirmed cause as fact costs you credibility when it turns out to be wrong, and anchors everyone else on your first guess. A concrete next-update time, which is the single highest-value line: it converts an anxious channel of people asking 'any news?' into people who will check back at 14:40, and you must post at that time even if the update is 'no change'. And named roles, so people know who is coordinating and who to ask without interrupting the person debugging. Two habits that follow: write for the least technical person who will read the channel, since exec and support readers need impact and ETA rather than service names; and keep the technical detail in a thread or the engineering channel, so the main update stays scannable. The instinct to build is that during an incident your job is to reduce the number of people who need to ask you questions.
keyTakeaway: Impact with a number, confirmed separated from suspected, a committed next-update time, and named roles. Then keep the commitment.

stem: Your service emits detailed logs and rich metrics, but debugging a slow request that crosses six services still takes hours. What is missing, and why do logs and metrics not cover it?

options.text: Distributed tracing — logs and metrics are per-service aggregates, and neither can reconstruct the causal path of one request across service boundaries
options.why: Metrics aggregate away the individual request and logs are scoped to one process, so neither answers 'where did *this* request spend its time'. Only a trace context propagated across hops stitches the spans into a single causal timeline.

options.text: Better log aggregation, so all six services' logs are searchable in one place
options.why: Centralised logging is necessary and you should have it, but without a shared correlation ID you are still manually matching timestamps across six services — which is exactly the hours-long process the stem describes.

options.text: Higher-cardinality metrics, so you can slice latency by endpoint and customer
options.why: High-cardinality dimensions genuinely help you find *which* requests are slow, and are underrated. But they still describe populations; they cannot show you the sequence of calls a single slow request made.

options.text: Profiling, to find which functions consume the time
options.why: Profiling answers where CPU goes inside one process, which is valuable once you know which service is at fault. In a six-service path, most latency is usually spent waiting on other services, which a profiler will not show you.

explanation: The three pillars answer different questions and do not substitute for one another. Metrics tell you *that* something is wrong and are cheap enough to keep forever — they are aggregates, so the individual request is gone by construction. Logs tell you what happened inside one process, in detail, but they stop at the process boundary. Traces tell you where a single request went and how long each hop took, which is the only one of the three that survives a service boundary. The mechanism is context propagation: a trace ID and span ID travel with the request in headers (W3C `traceparent` is the standard), each service records a span with parent linkage, and a backend assembles them into a waterfall. Once you have it, the six-service mystery becomes a picture. Two things to do beyond turning it on. Put the trace ID in every log line, which makes logs and traces navigable from each other and is the single highest-value integration. And sample intelligently — head sampling at a low rate misses the rare slow requests you actually care about, so use tail sampling to keep all traces that were slow or errored plus a small fraction of the rest. Worth knowing that the industry has largely converged on OpenTelemetry for all three signals, so instrument once against that rather than a vendor SDK.
keyTakeaway: Metrics say something is wrong, logs say what happened in one process, traces say where one request went. Only traces cross service boundaries.

stem: This runs on Postgres at the default isolation level (READ COMMITTED) and is meant to stop a doctor rota dropping below one on-call doctor. What can still go wrong?

options.text: Write skew — two doctors run this concurrently, each reads 2, each takes themselves off call, and the shift ends with zero
options.why: Both transactions read a snapshot showing two doctors on call, both pass the check, and they update *different* rows so nothing conflicts. READ COMMITTED and SNAPSHOT isolation both permit this because no two writes touch the same row.

options.text: A dirty read of another transaction's uncommitted update
options.why: Dirty reads are prevented at READ COMMITTED by definition — that is what the level guarantees, and Postgres never permits them at any level. Reaching for this suggests reading the level's name rather than its actual anomaly set.

options.text: A non-repeatable read, since the count could change between the SELECT and the UPDATE
options.why: Close, and it correctly identifies that the read is not stable. But naming it non-repeatable read misses the point: the failure needs *two* transactions writing different rows, which is the write-skew pattern rather than one transaction seeing changed data.

options.text: A deadlock between the two concurrent transactions
options.why: Deadlock requires the transactions to contend for the same locks in opposing orders. Here each updates a different row and neither blocks the other, which is precisely why the anomaly slips through undetected.

explanation: Write skew is the anomaly that snapshot isolation does not prevent, and it is the one most likely to be in your production code right now. The shape: two transactions read an overlapping set of rows, each makes a decision based on that read, and each writes to a *different* row. Nothing conflicts, both commit, and an invariant spanning multiple rows is violated.
