Because there is no write-write conflict, no lock, no deadlock and no error — the database is behaving exactly as documented — this class of bug is usually found in production, by a customer. There are three fixes. Use `SERIALIZABLE` isolation, which in Postgres uses SSI to detect the dangerous read-write dependency structure and aborts one transaction with a serialization failure — cheap to adopt, but you must add retry logic for 40001 errors. Take an explicit lock that materialises the conflict, with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` over the rows you read so the transactions serialise on them. Or restructure so the invariant lives in a single row or a constraint the database can enforce, such as a counter row updated atomically or an exclusion constraint. The habit worth building: whenever a check-then-write spans multiple rows, ask what happens if two of these run at once on different rows, because that is exactly the case your isolation level is not covering.
keyTakeaway: Write skew: two transactions read the same rows, write different ones, and break an invariant. Snapshot isolation allows it — use SERIALIZABLE or lock what you read.

references.label: Berenson et al., 'A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels'

stem: A bug meant 3 months of events were written with a wrong field. You must reprocess 400 million events into a downstream store, while live traffic of 2,000 events/second continues. What matters most in the design?

options.text: Throttling the backfill and keeping it on a separate path, so it cannot starve or overtake live processing
options.why: A backfill is a self-inflicted traffic surge of enormous size. Without a rate limit and isolation from the live path, it saturates the downstream store and turns a data-quality problem into a customer-facing outage.

options.text: Making the reprocessing exactly-once so no event is written twice
options.why: The right instinct is to make writes idempotent — which you should — but chasing exactly-once is the wrong framing. Backfills interleave with live writes by construction, so idempotent upserts keyed on event ID are the practical answer.

options.text: Running the backfill as fast as possible to minimise the window of incorrect data
options.why: This optimises the wrong variable. Three months of wrong data has already been tolerated; a few extra hours costs little, while saturating the downstream store costs an incident. Urgency here is almost always self-imposed.

options.text: Taking a maintenance window so the backfill runs without contention
options.why: Rarely available and rarely necessary. It also concentrates all the risk into one irreversible window with no ability to pause, inspect and resume — which is the opposite of how you want a 400-million-record operation to behave.

explanation: Backfills are one of the most reliable ways for a competent team to cause an outage, because the instinct is to treat them as a batch job rather than as production traffic. 400 million events at any meaningful rate dwarfs 2,000/second of live load, and the downstream store cannot tell the difference. The design checklist: rate limit the backfill explicitly and make the limit adjustable at runtime, so you can dial it down the moment live latency moves. Run it on separate workers with their own connection pool and, ideally, its own replica or partition, so it cannot exhaust resources the live path needs. Make writes idempotent upserts keyed on event ID, since backfill and live processing will overlap and you need last-writer semantics that are correct either way. Checkpoint progress durably so a failure resumes rather than restarts — at this volume, restarting from zero is not an option you want to discover you need. Make it resumable and killable, and actually test the kill switch before starting. Watch live SLIs, not backfill progress, as the primary signal of health. And critically, decide ordering: if a backfilled old event can overwrite a newer live one, you need version or timestamp comparison in the upsert, or the fix will corrupt fresh data. Run it on a 1% sample first and verify the output before committing to the full run.
keyTakeaway: A backfill is production traffic. Throttle it, isolate it, checkpoint it, make writes idempotent, and watch live SLIs rather than backfill progress.

references.label: Google SRE Workbook, ch. 12 'Introducing Non-Abstract Large System Design'

stem: What property must a CRDT's merge function have, and what is the practical limitation people discover too late?

options.text: Merge must be commutative, associative and idempotent — so order and duplication stop mattering. The limit is that many business rules cannot be expressed this way
options.why: Those three properties are what make replicas converge regardless of message order or redelivery, removing the need for coordination. The catch is that constraints like 'never below zero' or global uniqueness are inherently coordinating, so no CRDT can express them.

options.text: Merge must be deterministic given the same inputs. The limit is memory growth from tombstones
options.why: Determinism is necessary but far too weak — a deterministic merge that depends on argument order still diverges. Tombstone growth is a genuine and painful operational problem, but it is a consequence rather than the fundamental limit.

options.text: Merge must be reversible, so conflicting updates can be undone. The limit is storage overhead for history
options.why: CRDTs do not require reversibility and most are not reversible — a grow-only set cannot remove elements at all. This describes something closer to event sourcing with compensations than a convergent replicated data type.

options.text: Merge must be totally ordered by timestamp. The limit is clock skew between replicas
options.why: This describes last-write-wins, which is one specific (and lossy) register CRDT, not the general requirement. The point of CRDTs is precisely to avoid depending on a total order across replicas.

explanation: A CRDT converges because its merge forms a join-semilattice: commutative so order does not matter, associative so grouping does not matter, idempotent so redelivery does not matter. Given those, any two replicas that have seen the same set of updates — in any order, any number of times — hold the same state, which means you can accept writes anywhere with no coordination at all. That is a genuinely powerful property and it is why CRDTs underpin collaborative editors and offline-first sync. The limitation people meet late is expressiveness. Counters, sets, registers, sequences and maps all have CRDT forms, so you can build a lot. But any invariant requiring global agreement is out of reach by construction: 'the balance must never go negative' cannot be enforced without coordination, because two replicas each approving a withdrawal they can individually afford will merge into an overdraft, and merge cannot reject. Same for uniqueness constraints, capacity limits, and 'only one person can claim this'. The other practical costs: metadata growth, since removals need tombstones and causal context that must be garbage-collected carefully; and semantic surprises, like a remove-wins set discarding a concurrent add in a way users find baffling. The right instinct is to use CRDTs where concurrent edits are genuinely commutative and reach for coordination — a consensus group or a single-writer partition — where an invariant needs enforcing, rather than trying to make CRDTs cover the whole domain.
keyTakeaway: CRDT merges must be commutative, associative and idempotent — which buys coordination-free convergence but cannot express any invariant needing agreement.

references.label: Shapiro et al., 'Conflict-free Replicated Data Types'

stem: A service handles 500 requests/second with an average latency of 200ms. How many requests are in flight on average, and why does this number matter operationally?

options.text: 100 — it sets the minimum concurrency (threads, connections, pool slots) the service must support to sustain that throughput
options.why: Little's law gives L = λW = 500 × 0.2 = 100 concurrent requests. If your thread pool or connection pool is smaller than that, you cannot reach the throughput regardless of available CPU, and requests queue instead.

options.text: 500 — throughput is by definition the number of requests being handled at any moment
options.why: Confuses a rate with a quantity. 500/second is requests entering per unit time; the number resident in the system also depends on how long each one stays, which is what latency measures.

options.text: 2,500 — requests per second divided by latency in seconds
options.why: Divides where it should multiply. Dividing rate by time yields units of requests per second squared, which is not a quantity of anything — a units check catches this immediately.

options.text: It cannot be determined without knowing the number of servers and their thread counts
options.why: Little's law holds for any stable system regardless of its internal structure. Server and thread counts tell you the capacity available to hold those 100 requests, not how many there are.

explanation: Little's law — L = λW, where L is items in the system, λ is arrival rate and W is time in system — is the most useful piece of arithmetic in performance work, because it holds for any stable system without assumptions about arrival distribution or service order. Three ways it earns its keep. Sizing: at 500 rps and 200ms you need at least 100 concurrent slots, so a pool of 50 caps you at 250 rps no matter how much CPU you have — a surprising number of throughput ceilings are just this. Diagnosis: if you know two of the three quantities you can derive the third, so measuring in-flight count and throughput gives you latency for free, which is handy when latency instrumentation is missing. And prediction: if latency doubles under load and arrival rate holds, concurrency doubles, so a pool sized for the healthy case saturates precisely when the system is already struggling — which is how a modest latency regression becomes an outage. Apply it at every layer, since each has its own L: threads, database connections, HTTP client slots, queue consumers. The most common design mistake it exposes is sizing pools from steady-state latency rather than degraded latency, so pick your pool sizes against the worst latency you intend to survive, not the average you normally see.
keyTakeaway: L = λW. Concurrency needed equals throughput times latency — so size pools against degraded latency, not the healthy average.

references.label: Little, 'A Proof for the Queuing Formula L = λW'

stem: A dashboard shows mean API latency at a healthy 45ms and it has not moved in weeks. Support tickets about slowness are rising steadily. What is most likely happening?

options.text: The tail is degrading while the mean is dominated by fast requests — you need p95/p99 and per-endpoint breakdowns
options.why: A mean over a heavily skewed distribution is anchored by the bulk of fast requests, so a minority getting much slower barely moves it. Those slow requests are exactly the users who file tickets, which is why complaints and the dashboard disagree.

options.text: Users are complaining about perceived slowness caused by frontend rendering, not API latency
options.why: Worth ruling out, and client-side time genuinely dominates some experiences. But reaching for it before checking your own percentiles skips the cheapest available measurement and risks dismissing a real backend regression.

options.text: The metric is sampled and the sample is missing slow requests
options.why: Sampling bias is real when it drops long requests, and it is worth verifying how the metric is collected. It is a less common cause than the plain fact that a mean is insensitive to tails.

options.text: The dashboard's time window is too wide, smoothing over spikes
options.why: Wide windows do hide short spikes and shorter resolution helps. That would show as intermittent complaints correlated in time, though, rather than the steady rise the stem describes.

explanation: Latency distributions are heavily right-skewed, so the mean is a poor summary and a dangerous one to alert on. If 95% of requests take 20ms and 5% take 500ms, the mean is about 44ms — healthy-looking, while one user in twenty waits half a second. Worse, means hide bimodality entirely: a cache hit path at 5ms and a miss path at 800ms average to something neither path ever experiences. Three habits fix this. Alert on percentiles, not means — p99 for user-facing paths, and watch p99.9 if you fan out, since a request touching many services meets several tails. Break down by dimension: an endpoint, a customer, a region or a single host can degrade while the aggregate looks fine, which is the same gray-failure problem in metric form. And prefer histograms to pre-computed percentiles, because percentiles cannot be averaged across hosts or time buckets — averaging per-host p99s is a mathematically meaningless number that many dashboards display with a straight face. Two further points: track the count alongside the percentile, since a p99 over ten requests is noise; and remember that the user's experience is not one request but a session, so per-session worst-case latency often correlates with complaints far better than any per-request percentile.
keyTakeaway: Means hide tails and bimodality. Alert on percentiles from histograms, broken down per endpoint and host — and never average percentiles.

references.label: Gil Tene, 'How NOT to Measure Latency'

stem: This load test reports p99 latency of 80ms, but production at the same request rate shows p99 of 3 seconds. What is wrong with the test?

code.content:
latencies = []
for i in range(100_000):
    start = time.time()
    response = client.get(URL)      # blocking
    latencies.append(time.time() - start)
    time.sleep(0.01)                # target 100 rps

print(percentile(latencies, 99))

options.text: Coordinated omission — when the server stalls the client stops sending, so the requests that would have been slowest are never issued and never measured
options.why: The loop's send rate is coupled to the server's response time: a 2-second stall means roughly 200 requests are simply not sent, rather than being sent and recorded as very slow. The test systematically deletes exactly the data points that define the tail.

options.text: A single-threaded client cannot generate enough concurrency to reproduce production load
options.why: A genuine limitation — one connection cannot produce realistic concurrency, and you would want many workers. But adding threads without fixing the send-rate coupling reproduces the same omission in each of them.

options.text: `time.time()` has insufficient resolution for millisecond measurements
options.why: Resolution is adequate for millisecond timing on any modern platform, though `time.perf_counter()` is the better choice for durations. This is a code-quality nit rather than the reason the numbers are off by 40x.

options.text: 100,000 samples is too few to estimate a p99 accurately
options.why: 100,000 samples puts roughly 1,000 observations above p99, which is plenty for a stable estimate. Sample size is not the problem when the measurement itself is systematically biased.

explanation: Coordinated omission is the most common way load tests produce comforting lies. A closed-loop client — one that waits for a response before sending the next request — has its send rate throttled by the server's own slowness. When the server stalls for two seconds, an open-loop system with real users would have accumulated 200 waiting requests, each experiencing progressively worse latency; the closed-loop client instead sends nothing and records a single 2-second sample. The stall is measured once rather than 200 times, so it vanishes into the noise and the tail looks clean. The fix is to measure against the intended schedule rather than the actual send time: record latency as now minus when the request *should* have been sent, so a stall correctly attributes elevated latency to every request that was due during it. Better, use an open-loop generator that issues requests on a fixed schedule regardless of outstanding responses, which is what wrk2, Gatling and k6 do by default — and be aware that many older tools do not. The general lesson generalises beyond load testing: any measurement whose sampling rate is affected by the thing being measured is biased, usually in the flattering direction. Ask of any performance number, 'what would this instrument fail to record?', because the answer is almost always 'the bad cases'.
keyTakeaway: A client that waits before sending stops sending when the server stalls, deleting the tail it was meant to measure. Time from the intended send, not the actual one.

references.label: Gil Tene, 'How NOT to Measure Latency'

stem: An endpoint that returns 50 orders with their customer names takes 2.1 seconds. The database reports every query as under 1ms and total database time as 55ms. Where is the time going?

options.text: Per-query round-trip overhead across 51 sequential queries — network and driver latency dominate, not query execution
options.why: Fast individual queries with slow total time is the signature of round trips: 51 sequential calls at even 20-40ms each of network, connection handling and driver overhead accounts for the gap that execution time does not.

options.text: The database is under-indexed, so queries are slower than reported
options.why: Directly contradicted by the measurement — the database reports sub-millisecond execution. An index problem would show up as slow individual queries, which is the one thing the stem rules out.

options.text: Serialising 50 orders to JSON is the bottleneck
options.why: Serialising 50 modest objects takes single-digit milliseconds in any mainstream runtime. Worth profiling to confirm, but it cannot account for two seconds at this data volume.

options.text: Connection pool contention is forcing queries to wait for a free connection
options.why: Pool waits are a real cause of this symptom and worth checking, since wait time often is not counted as query time. But with sequential queries from one request you hold one connection throughout, so contention would require concurrent load the stem does not mention.

explanation: This is the N+1 problem, and the reason it survives review is that every individual query looks excellent. One query fetches the orders, then a query per order fetches its customer — 51 round trips, each cheap to execute and expensive to make. Latency here is dominated by the fixed cost of a round trip, so the fix is to reduce the count rather than optimise the queries. Fetch the customers in one query with an `IN` clause over the collected IDs and join in memory, or use a single SQL join, or use your ORM's eager-loading facility, which exists precisely for this. Two broader points worth carrying. First, this is a special case of a general rule: when many small operations are sequential, the per-operation overhead dominates and batching is the lever, whether the operations are queries, HTTP calls, or file reads. The same shape appears as chatty microservice calls, where a page render fans out to twenty services in sequence, and the same fix applies — batch or parallelise. Second, this class of bug is invisible to per-query monitoring and obvious in a distributed trace, which is a concrete argument for tracing: the waterfall shows 51 identical spans stacked in a row and the diagnosis takes seconds rather than hours. Guard against regressions by asserting on query count in tests, which is cheap and catches the ORM quietly reintroducing it.
keyTakeaway: Fast queries and a slow endpoint means round trips, not execution. Count the calls — and assert on query count in tests.

stem: A service running 20 pods has a database pool of 100 connections each. Under load, latency rises sharply and Postgres CPU is at 95% with most time in context switching. The team proposes raising the pool to 200. What should you argue?

options.text: Shrink the pools — 2,000 connections vastly exceeds what the database can execute in parallel, and the excess becomes contention rather than throughput
options.why: A database executes work in parallel up to roughly its core and disk concurrency; connections beyond that queue inside the database where you cannot see or control them, adding scheduling and lock contention. Fewer connections usually raises throughput and lowers latency.

options.text: Raise the pool as proposed, since latency under load indicates connection starvation
options.why: Latency rising with the database already at 95% CPU means the bottleneck is execution, not admission. Adding connections sends more concurrent work into a saturated engine, which deepens the contention that is causing the problem.

options.text: Add read replicas to spread the connection load
options.why: Replicas help if the workload is read-heavy and are worth considering. But they address capacity while leaving the pathological connection count in place, so the primary keeps thrashing and you have added infrastructure to avoid a configuration fix.

options.text: Move to a larger database instance so it can handle more concurrent connections
options.why: Scaling up buys headroom and will mask the symptom for a while. It is expensive, and it leaves a configuration that will degrade again at the next traffic increase because the ratio of connections to real parallelism is unchanged.

explanation: Connection pools are frequently sized by intuition — bigger seems safer — and the intuition is backwards. A database can genuinely execute only a limited number of statements in parallel, bounded by cores and disk concurrency; a common starting heuristic is a few times the core count. Connections beyond that do not add throughput because there is nothing left to run them on. They add cost: each is memory and a backend process, they contend on internal locks and buffers, and the operating system spends more time context-switching between them. The result is a throughput curve that rises, peaks, and then *falls* as concurrency grows, with latency rising throughout — so the team is on the far side of the peak and proposing to go further. The right move is to compute the total: pods times per-pod pool size is the number the database sees, and 2,000 is the figure to put in front of people. Size the total against the database's real parallelism, then divide by pod count. If that leaves each pod with too few, put a pooler such as PgBouncer in front in transaction mode, which decouples application connection count from database connection count entirely and is the standard fix once pod counts grow. This is also a good example of a broader instinct: when a resource is saturated, adding concurrency makes it worse, and the lever is admission control rather than more parallelism.
keyTakeaway: Multiply pool size by pod count and compare to the database's real parallelism. Past the peak, more connections cut throughput and raise latency.

stem: A product requirement says a search page must render in under 300ms at p95. The path is: edge, API gateway, search service, ranking service, and a database. How should you turn this into engineering constraints?

options.text: Allocate an explicit budget per hop that sums to under 300ms with headroom, and set each service's timeout and SLO from its allocation
options.why: Decomposing the end-to-end target gives every team a number they own and can test against, and it makes the timeout at each hop derivable rather than guessed. Without allocation, each service optimises locally and the total is discovered only in production.

options.text: Set a 300ms timeout at every hop, so no single service can exceed the budget
options.why: Guarantees the budget is blown: four hops each allowed 300ms can total 1.2 seconds. Timeouts must shrink down the chain, and a uniform timeout equal to the total is the classic way to make the requirement unenforceable.

options.text: Measure current end-to-end p95 and optimise the slowest service until the total is met
options.why: A reasonable tactical step once you have budgets, and profiling before optimising is right. As a strategy it lacks a stopping condition and no team knows whether their service is acceptable, so the target keeps drifting back.

options.text: Set the SLO at p95 300ms on the edge only, since that is what the user experiences
options.why: Correct about what matters to the user, and the edge SLO should exist. But an end-to-end number alone gives no team an actionable target, so when it is breached nobody knows whose budget was overspent.

explanation: A latency budget turns a product requirement into per-team constraints, and the act of allocating it is where the useful arguments happen. Decompose the path and assign each hop a share summing to meaningfully less than the target — leave 20-30% headroom, because budgets are spent at p95 while the components compose unevenly and you need room for growth. Each allocation then drives three concrete things: the service's own latency SLO, the timeout its caller sets on it, and the point at which someone is expected to do optimisation work. Several subtleties are worth knowing. Percentiles do not add — the p95 of a sum is not the sum of the p95s, and for independent hops the total is better than naive addition while for correlated hops it is worse. So treat the summed budget as a planning device and validate the composed number by measuring end to end. Account for what the decomposition omits: DNS, TLS handshake, queueing at each hop, and serialisation between them are real and frequently unbudgeted. And where the budget will not fit, the conversation becomes a design one — cache, precompute, parallelise independent hops instead of chaining them, or return partial results — which is exactly the discussion the budget was meant to force. The senior habit here is converting a single user-facing number into owned, testable constraints rather than a shared aspiration.
keyTakeaway: Decompose an end-to-end target into per-hop budgets with headroom, and derive each timeout and SLO from its allocation.

stem: A pipeline processes events one at a time at 1,200 events/second, with 90% of per-event time spent on a 15ms external API call. The team wants 10,000 events/second. What is the most effective change?

options.text: Increase concurrency on the I/O-bound call, and batch into the external API if it supports it — the work is waiting, not computing
options.why: When 90% of time is spent blocked on a network call, throughput is bounded by concurrency rather than CPU: Little's law says 10,000/s at 15ms needs about 150 in flight. Batching reduces the number of calls outright, which is better still.

options.text: Rewrite the hot path in a faster language to reduce per-event CPU cost
options.why: Optimises the 10% of time that is not the bottleneck. Even eliminating all local computation raises throughput by roughly a ninth, which is nowhere near the 8x the team needs — Amdahl's law caps the benefit hard.

options.text: Scale horizontally to 8 times as many workers
options.why: It would work and is sometimes the pragmatic answer, but it multiplies cost by eight to fix a problem caused by each worker sitting idle 90% of the time. Fixing the concurrency first usually makes most of that hardware unnecessary.

options.text: Add a cache in front of the external API to avoid repeat calls
options.why: Excellent if the calls repeat, and worth measuring the hit rate. The stem gives no indication of repetition, and for a pipeline of distinct events the hit rate is often near zero, so it is a bet rather than a fix.

explanation: The discipline being tested is identifying what a workload is actually bound by before optimising, because the wrong classification wastes the whole effort. Here 90% of time is spent waiting on the network, which makes this I/O-bound: the CPU is idle and the constraint is how many requests you keep in flight. Little's law sizes it — 10,000 per second at 15ms each requires around 150 concurrent calls — so the change is to run those calls concurrently via async I/O or a worker pool, not to make the local code faster. Amdahl's law bounds the alternative: with 10% of time in local computation, infinite local speedup yields about 1.11x. Batching is better than concurrency where the API supports it, because it removes round trips entirely rather than overlapping them; 100 events per call at 10,000/s is 100 calls per second instead of 10,000, which also spares the downstream. When batching, make the trade explicit — batches add latency while they fill, so pick a size and a max-wait timeout deliberately, and remember a failed batch fails many events at once, so design partial-failure handling. Finally, before raising concurrency to 150, check that the downstream will accept it: the fastest way to turn a throughput project into an incident is to point 150 concurrent connections at a service sized for 12.
keyTakeaway: Classify the bottleneck before optimising. I/O-bound work needs concurrency or batching; making the idle 10% faster is capped by Amdahl's law.

references.label: Amdahl, 'Validity of the single processor approach'

stem: A team sets an availability SLO of 99.9% over 30 days and has consumed 80% of its error budget by day 10. What should that trigger?

options.text: A deliberate slowdown of risky changes and a shift of effort toward reliability until the budget recovers
options.why: The budget exists to convert reliability from an argument into a policy: spending it fast is the agreed signal to trade feature velocity for stability. Acting on it is the entire point, and a budget nobody responds to is decoration.

options.text: Raising the SLO to 99.95% so the team takes reliability more seriously
options.why: Backwards — tightening the target while already failing it makes the budget more negative and the signal less usable. SLO targets should reflect what users need, not be used as a motivational device.

options.text: An incident review, since 80% consumption indicates a major outage occurred
options.why: Worth doing if a single large event caused it, and you should know which. But budget consumption can equally come from steady low-level errors, and the response to a depleted budget is a policy change rather than only a retrospective.

options.text: Nothing yet — the budget is not exhausted, so the team is within its agreed reliability target
options.why: Technically true and operationally naive. At this burn rate the budget is gone before the window ends, so waiting for exhaustion means reacting when there is no margin left to protect users.

explanation: An error budget converts reliability from a matter of opinion into an agreed currency. If the SLO is 99.9% over 30 days, roughly 43 minutes of unavailability is not a failure — it is the budget, and it exists to be spent on shipping. That reframing is what makes the mechanism valuable: it gives the team explicit permission to take risk while the budget is healthy, and an unarguable trigger to stop when it is not. Consuming 80% in a third of the window is a burn rate far above sustainable, so the agreed response engages: freeze or slow risky deploys, redirect effort to the causes, and require a higher bar for changes until the trend recovers. For this to work, three things must be true. The policy must be agreed in advance with product, because negotiating a freeze during a crisis never goes well. The SLO must reflect genuine user need — an SLO set higher than users require burns effort for nothing and gets ignored, which is worse than not having one. And you should alert on burn rate rather than raw budget consumption, using multiple windows so a fast burn pages immediately while a slow steady burn opens a ticket. Also worth remembering that the point of an SLO is to be occasionally missed: if you never consume the budget, the target is too loose or you are over-investing in reliability at the expense of everything else.
keyTakeaway: An error budget is permission to take risk, and a pre-agreed trigger to stop. Alert on burn rate, and act before it is exhausted.

references.label: Google SRE Workbook, ch. 5 'Alerting on SLOs'

stem: An on-call rotation receives about 40 pages a week. Roughly 3 require action. Engineers are exhausted and have started acknowledging pages without reading them. What is the correct framing of the problem?

options.text: The alerts are measuring causes rather than symptoms — page on user-visible impact, and route everything else to a ticket or dashboard
options.why: A 7% actionability rate means most alerts fire on conditions that do not affect users, such as a single host's CPU or a transient error blip. Paging only on symptoms that breach an SLO collapses the volume and restores the meaning of a page.

options.text: Alert thresholds are too tight and should be raised until the volume is manageable
options.why: Raising thresholds on the same cause-based alerts reduces noise by making each alert less sensitive, which trades false positives for missed real problems. It treats volume as the disease rather than as the symptom of alerting on the wrong things.

options.text: The rotation is understaffed; more engineers would reduce the per-person burden
options.why: Spreads a broken process over more people and normalises it. It also does nothing about the acknowledged-without-reading behaviour, which is the genuinely dangerous outcome because it will eventually swallow a real page.

options.text: The team needs better runbooks so pages can be resolved faster
options.why: Runbooks are valuable and every page should have one. Making it faster to dismiss 37 unnecessary pages is optimising a process that should not exist, and the fatigue is caused by interruption rather than by resolution time.

explanation: The diagnostic number here is actionability: if fewer than most pages result in action, the alerting is broken, and the specific failure is almost always alerting on causes rather than symptoms. Cause-based alerts — high CPU on a host, elevated memory, a queue above some depth, a single failed health check — fire constantly and usually mean nothing, because systems are designed to absorb exactly those conditions. Symptom-based alerts fire when users are affected: error rate breaching the SLO, latency past the budget, a critical path failing. Reserve paging for those, and route everything else to tickets, dashboards, or nothing at all. The behaviour described in the stem is the part to take seriously: acknowledging without reading is a rational adaptation to noise, and it means the next real page will also be dismissed. That is a safety failure, not a discipline failure, and it will not be fixed by asking people to be more careful. Practical rules that follow: every page must be actionable, urgent, and have a documented response — if any of the three is missing it is not a page; review every page in a weekly triage and delete or downgrade the ones that were not actionable, which is the single highest-value recurring meeting an on-call team can hold; and track pages per shift as a metric someone owns, because alert volume grows silently unless something pushes back on it.
keyTakeaway: Page on user-visible symptoms, not causes. If most pages are not actionable, people stop reading them — and that is a safety failure, not a discipline one.

references.label: Google SRE Book, ch. 6 'Monitoring Distributed Systems'

stem: A service deploys twice a day to 60 pods. Two recent incidents were caused by bad deploys that took 25 minutes to detect and roll back. What change gives the most risk reduction for the least effort?

options.text: Canary the deploy to a small share of traffic with automated metric comparison and automatic rollback on regression
options.why: It bounds the blast radius to a fraction of users and removes the human detection delay that dominated both incidents. Automating the comparison and rollback is what turns 25 minutes into a couple of minutes without asking anyone to watch a dashboard.

options.text: Add more integration tests so bad builds are caught before deploy
options.why: Always worth doing, but the failures that reach production are by definition the ones tests did not model — usually production data, scale or configuration. Testing raises the floor; it does not bound the damage when something still gets through.

options.text: Move to blue-green deployment so rollback is instant
options.why: Rollback does become fast, which helps, but blue-green still exposes 100% of traffic the moment you cut over. It solves the recovery half of the problem while leaving the blast radius and the detection delay untouched.

options.text: Deploy less frequently, batching changes into a weekly release
options.why: Makes things worse in the way teams consistently underestimate: larger batches mean more changes per deploy, so each failure is harder to attribute and riskier to roll back. Deploy frequency and stability are positively correlated, not opposed.

explanation: Two independent quantities determine deploy risk: how many users a bad change reaches, and how long it takes to stop. Canarying attacks both. Route a small share of traffic — often one pod, or 1-5% — to the new version, compare its error rate and latency against the stable version automatically, and promote or roll back based on that comparison rather than on someone watching. Automating the decision is the part that matters, because the 25-minute detection delay in the stem is human latency, and a canary that requires a person to notice reproduces it. Practical details that decide whether this works: compare canary against control concurrently rather than against yesterday's baseline, since traffic patterns shift; give the canary enough traffic and enough time to produce a statistically meaningful signal, as a canary at 0.1% for two minutes tells you nothing; and make sure the metrics you compare are the ones that reflect user harm rather than resource usage. Note also that the last option is a real trap — the intuition that fewer deploys means less risk is strong and wrong, and the DORA research consistently finds that frequent small deploys correlate with *better* stability, because each change is small enough to reason about and to revert. Pair canarying with feature flags so risky behaviour can be disabled without a deploy at all, which decouples release from deploy and gives you a second, faster off switch.
keyTakeaway: Deploy risk is blast radius times detection time. Canary with automated comparison and rollback attacks both; deploying less often attacks neither.

stem: A postmortem for a 3-hour outage concludes: 'Root cause: an engineer deployed a config change without following the review process. Action: remind the team to follow the process.' What is wrong with this?

options.text: It stops at human error instead of asking why the system permitted it — the useful questions are why the change was possible to make unreviewed and why it took 3 hours to detect
options.why: Naming a person as the cause ends the investigation exactly where it should start. A system that allows an unreviewed config change to reach production and take three hours to surface has several fixable properties, none of which a reminder addresses.

options.text: It does not identify a single root cause precisely enough; the analysis should continue until one is found
options.why: Chases a fiction. Real incidents in complex systems have multiple contributing conditions that only combine to cause harm, and insisting on a single root cause tends to produce whichever one is easiest to name — usually a person.

options.text: The action item is not assigned to a named owner with a deadline
options.why: A genuine process gap, and unowned actions do quietly evaporate. But assigning an owner to 'remind the team' just produces an owned reminder, so it fixes the tracking of a worthless action.

options.text: It does not quantify the customer impact of the outage
options.why: Impact quantification belongs in a postmortem and helps prioritise the follow-up work. It is a missing section rather than the flaw in the reasoning, which is that the analysis terminated on a person.

explanation: 'Human error' is where a bad postmortem stops and a good one starts. People make mistakes constantly and systems that depend on them not doing so are the actual defect, so a conclusion naming an individual has skipped the analysis. The productive questions here: why was it possible to deploy config without review — is the control advisory rather than enforced? Why did it take three hours to detect — what would have caught it in three minutes? Why did a single config change take the whole service down — is there validation, staged rollout, or a fast revert? What made the change look reasonable to a competent engineer at the time, since that reveals a genuine gap between the system's behaviour and its mental model. Each of those yields an action that changes the system rather than exhorting people. The blameless framing is not politeness for its own sake: if naming the person is the outcome, engineers learn to be defensive, near-misses go unreported, and you lose the information that would have prevented the next incident. Two practical habits. Write what happened as a timeline with what people believed at each point, not only what was true, because responders act on their understanding and that is where detection and diagnosis improvements come from. And treat the action list as the deliverable — a postmortem with excellent analysis and no owned, dated, prioritised changes has produced a document rather than a safer system.
keyTakeaway: Human error is the start of the analysis, not the end. Ask what made the mistake possible and what made it slow to detect.

references.label: Allspaw, 'Blameless PostMortems and a Just Culture'

stem: A service handles 8,000 rps at peak on 40 pods, each maxing at roughly 400 rps before latency degrades. Marketing expects a campaign to triple traffic in 6 weeks. Autoscaling is enabled with a 3-minute scale-up. What is the main risk and what would you do?

options.text: Autoscaling cannot absorb a fast ramp and the dependencies may not scale with you — load test at 3x, pre-scale for the event, and verify every downstream's headroom
options.why: A 3-minute scale-up is far slower than a campaign spike, so the first minutes run on existing capacity. And scaling your pods 3x pushes 3x load onto databases, caches and third parties that have their own ceilings and often cannot scale at all.

options.text: 40 pods at 400 rps each gives 16,000 rps of headroom, so 24,000 rps requires roughly 60 pods — configure the maximum and rely on autoscaling
options.why: The arithmetic is right and the conclusion is too comfortable. It assumes the pods are the only constraint, that scaling arrives in time, and that per-pod capacity holds at 3x, none of which is established without a test.

options.text: The risk is cost — running 3x capacity is expensive, so use aggressive scale-down policies to control spend
options.why: Cost is a real consideration and scale-down policy matters. Optimising spend before establishing that the system survives the event is the wrong order, and aggressive scale-down during a spiky campaign causes repeated cold-start thrash.

options.text: Six weeks is enough time to optimise per-pod throughput, reducing the number of pods needed
options.why: Efficiency work is valuable and may be worth doing. As the primary response to a dated event it is a gamble on an uncertain outcome, and it does nothing about dependency limits or the ramp speed that autoscaling cannot meet.

explanation: Capacity planning fails in two predictable places, and both are about what the naive arithmetic omits. The first is time: autoscaling is a control loop with delay — metric collection, decision, scheduling, image pull, warm-up, readiness — and three minutes of that is an eternity against a marketing spike that arrives in seconds when an email lands. Whatever happens in those first minutes happens on current capacity, so pre-scale ahead of known events rather than trusting the loop, and make sure the scale-up policy is aggressive enough to matter afterwards. The second is dependencies: tripling your own throughput triples the load you place on databases, caches, queues and third-party APIs, and those often cannot scale on the same timescale or at all. A connection pool that was comfortable at 8,000 rps may be pathological at 24,000, and a vendor may simply rate-limit you. So the work is: load test at the target rate against a production-like environment and find what breaks first, because it is rarely the thing you expected; enumerate every downstream and confirm its headroom, including quotas and rate limits you do not control; pre-scale before the event and hold it; and prepare graceful degradation so that if you are wrong, non-essential features shed load rather than the checkout path failing. Finally, agree in advance what you will turn off — deciding that during the spike is how a capacity problem becomes an outage.
keyTakeaway: Autoscaling is a delayed control loop and your dependencies may not scale at all. Load test at target, pre-scale for known events, and check every downstream's ceiling.

stem: Why are configuration changes disproportionately represented among large-scale outages, compared to code changes?

options.text: Config typically bypasses the safeguards code goes through — tests, canaries, staged rollout — while often applying globally and instantly
options.why: Teams invest heavily in the code pipeline and then let config propagate through a different path with none of it. A change that is untested, unstaged and global by default is the highest-risk shape of change a system can accept.

options.text: Configuration is written by operations staff who are less familiar with the system's internals
options.why: Attributes the pattern to people rather than to the pipeline, and in most modern teams the same engineers write both. It also points at training as the remedy, which does not address the missing safeguards.

options.text: Config formats like YAML are error-prone and lack type safety
options.why: Format hazards are real — indentation errors and surprising type coercion do cause incidents — and schema validation helps. But a typo caught by validation is a small subset of config-caused outages, most of which are valid values with bad consequences.

options.text: Configuration changes are made more frequently than code changes, so they cause proportionally more incidents
options.why: Frequency alone would predict proportional representation, not the disproportionate share observed. The distinguishing factor is that each config change carries more risk, not that there are more of them.

explanation: Configuration is code that skipped the pipeline. A code change is reviewed, tested, built, deployed to staging, canaried, and rolled out gradually with automatic rollback. A config change is frequently edited in a console or a repo with no equivalent gate, applied to every instance at once, and takes effect immediately — and because it feels small, it attracts less scrutiny precisely when it deserves more. Several of the largest publicly-documented internet outages have this shape: a valid-looking config value propagating globally in seconds. The remedy is to give config the same pipeline as code. Version it in source control with review. Validate it against a schema, and beyond schema, validate semantics — a rate limit of zero, a timeout of zero, an empty allow-list are all schema-valid and catastrophic. Roll it out in stages with the same canary and automatic rollback as code, which requires the system to support partial config states and is the part teams skip. Make rollback fast and, critically, test that rollback works, since some config changes are not reversible in effect even when reversible in value. And build a break-glass path that does not depend on the config system, because the failure mode you must survive is config that breaks the mechanism used to fix config. A useful design instinct: prefer config that fails closed toward the previous known-good value rather than toward an empty or default state, since 'no rules loaded' usually means 'allow everything' or 'deny everything', and both are incidents.
keyTakeaway: Config is code that skipped the pipeline — global, instant, unstaged. Give it review, semantic validation, canaries and tested rollback.

references.label: Google SRE Workbook, ch. 14 'Configuration Design and Best Practices'

stem: A social feed is served from 6 read replicas lagging 50-800ms behind the primary. Users report their own new posts vanishing on refresh, and occasionally seeing a comment appear before the post it replies to. Reads are 50x writes, so routing everything to the primary is not viable. What do you implement?

options.text: Session guarantees — pin a writing session to a replica caught up past its last write position, and track causal dependencies for the comment ordering
options.why: The two symptoms are distinct guarantees: the vanishing post is read-your-writes, the out-of-order comment is causal consistency. Both are obtainable per session without forcing all reads to the primary, which preserves the read scaling you need.

options.text: Route reads to the primary for 2 seconds after any write by that user, then return to replicas
options.why: A common and workable heuristic for read-your-writes, and cheap to build. But a fixed window is a guess — it fails when lag exceeds it and wastes primary capacity when it does not — and it does nothing for the cross-user comment ordering.

options.text: Reduce replication lag by tuning the replicas until staleness is imperceptible
options.why: Lower lag reduces how often anomalies occur without removing them, so the bug becomes rarer and harder to reproduce. Lag is also not fully controllable, since it spikes exactly under the load when users are most active.

options.text: Serve the feed from a cache written at the same time as the primary, bypassing replication
options.why: Reintroduces the dual-write problem — cache and database can disagree on any failure — and a cache is another replica with its own staleness. It relocates the consistency problem rather than solving it.

explanation: The valuable move is recognising two different anomalies in one report, because they need different mechanisms. A user not seeing their own post is read-your-writes; a comment appearing before its parent is a causality violation across users. For read-your-writes, the robust implementation is to return the write's log position or timestamp to the client, carry it in the session, and require any replica serving that session to have applied at least that position — routing to another replica or briefly to the primary if none has caught up. That is precise where a fixed time window is a guess, and it degrades gracefully under lag spikes. For causal consistency you need dependency tracking: the comment carries the version of the post it depends on, and a replica that has not yet applied that version either waits or the read is routed elsewhere. Monotonic reads — never going backwards in time — comes almost free by pinning a session to one replica, and is worth having since bouncing between replicas of differing lag produces bizarre user-visible flicker. Two engineering notes: expose replication position through your data layer rather than scattering staleness logic through the application, and treat lag as an SLI with alerting, because every one of these mechanisms degrades toward the primary and a lag spike therefore becomes a load spike on the one node you cannot scale.
keyTakeaway: Vanishing own writes and out-of-order replies are different guarantees. Track write position per session for the first, causal dependencies for the second.

references.label: Terry et al., 'Session Guarantees for Weakly Consistent Replicated Data'

stem: A leaderless store uses read repair to fix divergent replicas. Why is read repair alone insufficient, and what complements it?

options.text: It only repairs data that is read, so rarely-read keys diverge indefinitely — you need a background anti-entropy process such as Merkle-tree comparison
options.why: Repair is a side effect of reads, so coverage follows the access distribution. Cold keys are never compared, and durability quietly erodes on exactly the data nobody is watching, which is where a lost replica becomes lost data.

options.text: Read repair is asynchronous, so the reader still receives stale data before the repair completes
options.why: True of the common asynchronous variant, and blocking read repair exists to address it. That concerns the freshness of one read rather than the long-term convergence problem the question is about.

options.text: Read repair cannot resolve conflicts between concurrent writes, only stale ones
options.why: Conflict resolution is genuinely a separate concern needing version vectors or CRDTs. But read repair does apply whatever resolution policy the store defines, so this describes a limit of the policy rather than of repair coverage.

options.text: Read repair increases read latency, so it is usually disabled in production
options.why: It adds modest overhead and is typically left on rather than disabled. Framing it as a performance cost misses that the problem is coverage — repair does not run where reads do not go.

explanation: Read repair is opportunistic: when a read gathers responses from several replicas and notices one is stale, it writes back the newer value. It is nearly free because the comparison rides along with work you were doing anyway, and for hot keys it keeps replicas tightly converged. The gap is that its coverage is exactly your read distribution, and real access patterns are heavily skewed — a large share of keys may go unread for months. Those keys accumulate divergence from dropped writes, hinted handoffs that never completed, and replicas that were down during a write. Nothing notices, and durability degrades silently until a node loss turns a repairable divergence into permanent data loss. Anti-entropy closes it by comparing replicas systematically in the background. The efficient technique is a Merkle tree per replica range: hash the data hierarchically and exchange only the top hashes, descending only into subtrees that differ, so identical ranges cost one comparison and divergent ones are found in logarithmic work. This is what Dynamo-lineage systems run as periodic repair. Two operational points worth knowing: repair is expensive in I/O and network, so it needs scheduling and throttling like any background job competing with live traffic, and it must actually be run — a repair job that has been failing silently for months is a common and unpleasant discovery. The general principle transfers beyond storage: any consistency mechanism triggered by access leaves the unaccessed portion unprotected, so pair opportunistic repair with systematic sweeps.
keyTakeaway: Read repair covers only what gets read, so cold data diverges silently. Pair it with scheduled Merkle-tree anti-entropy — and check the job is actually running.

references.label: DeCandia et al., 'Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store'

stem: A service calls five downstream dependencies from a shared thread pool of 200. One dependency slows from 50ms to 8 seconds. Within two minutes, all endpoints of the service are failing, including those that never touch the slow dependency. Why?

options.text: Resource pool exhaustion — slow calls hold threads far longer, so one dependency consumes the entire shared pool and starves every other code path
options.why: At 8 seconds per call, threads are held 160 times longer, so the calls to that one dependency accumulate until they occupy all 200. Unrelated endpoints then cannot obtain a thread, and a single dependency's degradation becomes total failure.

options.text: The slow dependency is causing memory pressure that triggers garbage collection across the service
options.why: Queued requests do consume memory and GC pressure can follow. But the mechanism that takes down unrelated endpoints in two minutes is the exhaustion of a shared, countable resource, not a gradual memory effect.

options.text: Cascading failure from retries against the slow dependency amplifying load
options.why: Retries would amplify pressure on the slow dependency and are worth checking. They do not explain why endpoints with no relationship to it fail, which requires something shared between the paths.

options.text: The health check is timing out, so the load balancer removed the instance from rotation
options.why: A plausible late-stage consequence once threads are exhausted, and it would compound the outage. It is downstream of the actual mechanism rather than its cause.

explanation: A shared resource pool couples everything that uses it, so the blast radius of any one dependency's degradation is the entire service. The arithmetic is stark: a call that took 50ms and now takes 8 seconds holds its thread 160 times longer, so a modest request rate to that dependency saturates a 200-thread pool in seconds. Every other endpoint then queues for a thread it will never get, and a partial dependency failure presents as total service failure. Bulkheads fix this by partitioning the resource — named after ship compartments that stop one breach sinking the vessel. Give each dependency its own bounded pool sized to its expected concurrency, so calls to the slow one queue and fail within their own compartment while the rest of the service continues. The right size comes from Little's law: expected rate times expected latency, plus headroom. Combine it with a timeout short enough that a hung call cannot hold a slot for long, and a circuit breaker so sustained failure stops consuming the compartment at all — the three together are what make a dependency's failure survivable rather than fatal. Two extensions worth carrying: bulkhead by tenant or by request class as well as by dependency, so one large customer or one expensive endpoint cannot starve the rest; and remember that connection pools, semaphores, and queue slots are all the same kind of shared countable resource, so the analysis applies wherever one exists.
keyTakeaway: A shared pool couples every caller to the slowest dependency. Give each its own bounded compartment, sized by rate times latency.

stem: You need to detect whether two updates to the same record were concurrent or one caused the other. Lamport timestamps are proposed. What is the limitation?

options.text: Lamport timestamps only guarantee that a cause has a lower number than its effect — a lower number does not prove causality, so concurrency is undetectable; vector clocks are needed
options.why: The implication runs one way only: if A caused B then A's timestamp is lower, but a lower timestamp can equally mean the events were concurrent. Vector clocks track a counter per node, so incomparable vectors positively identify concurrency.

options.text: Lamport timestamps can collide between nodes, requiring a node ID tiebreak
options.why: Collisions do happen and a node ID does give a deterministic total order. That is about producing an arbitrary tiebreak, not about the missing ability to distinguish 'happened before' from 'happened concurrently'.

options.text: Lamport timestamps drift from wall-clock time, making them hard to interpret in logs
options.why: They are logical counters with no relation to wall time by design, which is a readability inconvenience that hybrid logical clocks address. It has nothing to do with the causality detection the question asks about.

options.text: Lamport timestamps require synchronised clocks across nodes to be comparable
options.why: The opposite — their whole appeal is needing no clock synchronisation at all, since they are counters incremented on local events and message receipt. This confuses them with physical timestamps.

explanation: Lamport timestamps give a total order consistent with causality, which sounds like more than it is. The guarantee is one-directional: if A happens-before B then L(A) < L(B). The converse fails, so observing L(A) < L(B) tells you either that A caused B or that they were concurrent, and you cannot tell which. That is fine when you only need *an* order everyone agrees on — deterministic tiebreaking, deciding a winner — and useless when you need to know whether a genuine conflict occurred. Vector clocks carry a counter per node. Comparing two vectors gives three outcomes: A dominates B on every entry, so A happened after; B dominates A, so B happened after; or each exceeds the other somewhere, which means they were concurrent and you have a real conflict to resolve. That third case is the entire point, and it is why Dynamo-lineage stores use version vectors to surface conflicting writes to the application rather than silently picking one. The cost is size — vectors grow with the number of writing nodes, which is why implementations bound them with client IDs rather than server IDs, prune entries, and use dotted version vectors to avoid the sibling explosion. Worth knowing the third option too: hybrid logical clocks pair a physical timestamp with a logical counter, preserving happens-before while staying close to wall time, which makes them far more debuggable in logs. Choose by what you need: a total order, conflict detection, or human-readable ordering.
keyTakeaway: Lamport gives an order consistent with causality but cannot detect concurrency. Vector clocks can, because incomparable vectors mean a real conflict.

references.label: Lamport, 'Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System'

stem: A streaming job computes hourly revenue totals. Numbers are correct most of the time, but after any consumer lag or a mobile client syncing offline data, an hour's total is understated and never corrects. What is the underlying mistake?

options.text: Windowing on processing time rather than event time — events are assigned to the hour they arrived, not the hour they occurred
options.why: Processing-time windows bucket by arrival, so anything delayed lands in the wrong hour: lagged or offline-synced events are counted against a later window while the hour they belong to has already closed and been reported.

options.text: The consumer is not committing offsets correctly, so events are lost during lag
options.why: Offset mishandling causes loss or duplication and is worth verifying. It would not correlate specifically with delayed arrival, and it would tend to affect totals randomly rather than always understating the hour the events belonged to.

options.text: The window size is too small to accommodate variable throughput
options.why: Window size determines granularity, not correctness under delay. A larger window reduces how often a late event crosses a boundary but leaves the same defect for anything arriving after the window closes.

options.text: Clock skew between producers means event timestamps are unreliable
options.why: Producer clock skew is a genuine hazard for event-time processing and needs bounding. But it would produce small random misassignment, not the systematic understatement that tracks exactly with arrival delay.

explanation: Event time is when something happened; processing time is when your system saw it. They diverge constantly — consumer lag, retries, network partitions, mobile clients that were offline for a day — and the choice between them decides whether your numbers are correct or merely timely. Windowing on processing time is simple and gives results at predictable moments, but it is not reproducible: replaying the same stream produces different windows, and any delay silently moves revenue between hours. Windowing on event time is correct and reproducible, at the cost of needing a policy for lateness, because you can never be sure everything has arrived. That policy is the watermark: a moving assertion that no events older than time T are expected. When the watermark passes a window's end the window is emitted; events arriving after that are late. You then choose explicitly what to do with them — drop them and track the count as a metric, hold windows open for a defined allowed-lateness period and re-emit updated results, or route them to a side output for reconciliation. For revenue, dropping silently is the wrong answer, which is exactly the bug in the stem. Two practical notes: make the downstream store idempotent and keyed by window so re-emitted results correct rather than duplicate; and treat the watermark delay as an explicit latency-versus-completeness trade you tune with data, since a generous watermark is accurate and slow while a tight one is fast and lossy.
keyTakeaway: Window on event time, not arrival time, and make lateness an explicit policy — dropped late events silently understate closed windows.

stem: This measures how long an operation took and enforces a timeout. What can go wrong?

options.text: `currentTimeMillis` is a wall clock that NTP can step forward or backward, so elapsed time can be wrong or negative — a monotonic source like `System.nanoTime` is required for durations
options.why: Wall clocks are adjusted by NTP and can jump in either direction, so a correction during `doWork()` corrupts the measurement. A backward step produces a negative elapsed value and a forward step can trigger a spurious timeout on work that was fast.

options.text: Millisecond resolution is too coarse for accurate timing of fast operations
options.why: A real precision limitation for sub-millisecond work, and nanoTime resolves it too. But coarse resolution produces small quantisation error rather than the wrong-by-seconds or negative results a clock step causes.

options.text: The timeout is checked after the work completes, so it cannot actually interrupt a hung operation
options.why: Genuinely important and arguably a worse bug in practice — this detects overrun rather than preventing it, and a truly hung `doWork()` never reaches the check. It is a control-flow flaw rather than the measurement flaw the clock choice introduces.

options.text: `System.currentTimeMillis` is not thread-safe and may return inconsistent values under concurrency
options.why: It is thread-safe and simply reads the system clock. This invents a concurrency hazard where the real hazard is that the underlying clock is externally mutable.

explanation: There are two kinds of clock and using the wrong one is a durable source of confusing bugs. A wall clock reports civil time, is meaningful across machines, and is adjusted — NTP slews it continuously and steps it when the drift is large, leap seconds are smeared or stepped depending on configuration, and a VM resuming from a snapshot can jump substantially. A monotonic clock counts from an arbitrary origin, is meaningless across machines and across reboots, and never goes backwards. The rule that follows: use wall clocks for timestamps you will display, store, or compare across machines; use monotonic clocks for every duration, timeout, rate limit, and backoff calculation. `System.nanoTime` in Java, `time.monotonic()` in Python, `Instant::now` in Rust, `clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC)` in C. Go is unusual and helpful here — `time.Now()` carries a monotonic reading used automatically by `Sub`, though it is stripped by serialisation, which is why durations computed from marshalled timestamps lose the protection. The failure this causes is nasty because it is rare and unreproducible: a timeout fires on a fast operation, a rate limiter lets everything through, a backoff sleeps for hours, all because a clock moved during a window of a few milliseconds. The secondary flaw in the code is worth internalising too — measuring elapsed time after the fact detects an overrun but cannot enforce a deadline, which needs cancellation, a context deadline, or an interruptible call.
keyTakeaway: Wall clocks are adjustable and can step backwards. Every duration, timeout and backoff must come from a monotonic source.

stem: Why is total order broadcast — every node delivering the same messages in the same order — considered equivalent in difficulty to consensus?

options.text: Each can implement the other: agreeing on the next message in the sequence is one consensus decision, and consensus can be built by proposing values into a totally ordered log
options.why: The reduction runs both ways, which is what equivalence means. That is precisely how Raft and Multi-Paxos work — a replicated log is total order broadcast, and each entry is one consensus instance — so neither problem can be easier than the other.

options.text: Both require synchronised clocks to establish a global ordering of events
options.why: Neither requires clock synchronisation; both are solved with logical ordering and quorums. Introducing clocks would add a timing assumption that consensus algorithms deliberately avoid for safety.

options.text: Both are impossible in asynchronous networks by the FLP result, so both must use timeouts
options.why: FLP rules out guaranteed termination with deterministic algorithms under one crash, which is why practical systems use timeouts for liveness. That shared impossibility does not establish the mutual reduction that makes them equivalent.

options.text: Both require a majority quorum, so they have the same fault tolerance characteristics
options.why: They do share quorum-based implementations and tolerance properties, but sharing an implementation technique is not equivalence. Two problems can use majorities without either being reducible to the other.

explanation: Equivalence here is a formal statement: given a solution to one, you can construct a solution to the other. Total order broadcast from consensus is direct — run a consensus instance for each slot in a sequence, deciding which message occupies it, and every node delivers the agreed sequence. Consensus from total order broadcast is equally direct — every node broadcasts its proposal, and all nodes decide on the first message delivered, which is the same everywhere by the total order property. So neither is easier, and any lower bound or impossibility for one applies to the other. This matters practically more than it sounds. It tells you that anything requiring all nodes to agree on an order of operations — a replicated state machine, a linearizable database, a distributed lock service, leader election — is a consensus problem and carries consensus costs: a majority quorum, at least one round trip to that majority per decision, and unavailability when a majority is unreachable. So when a design says 'all replicas process operations in the same order', you should immediately price in those costs rather than assuming it is a cheap ordering trick. The corollary is the useful one for design: if you can avoid needing a total order — by partitioning so that ordering is only required within a partition, by making operations commutative so order stops mattering, or by accepting causal rather than total order — you escape consensus entirely and get a far cheaper, more available system.
keyTakeaway: Total order broadcast and consensus reduce to each other. Any design needing all nodes to agree on an order carries the full cost of consensus.

references.label: Chandra & Toueg, 'Unreliable Failure Detectors for Reliable Distributed Systems'

stem: A fraud detection job must react within 5 seconds of a transaction, but roughly 2% of events arrive up to 60 seconds late due to mobile connectivity. Waiting 60 seconds for completeness is unacceptable. How do you resolve this?

options.text: Emit a fast provisional result at 5 seconds and revise it when late events arrive, making downstream consumers handle updates
options.why: It refuses the false choice by separating latency from completeness: act on what you have, then correct. This requires downstream idempotency and a revision path, which is the real engineering cost and is usually worth paying.

options.text: Set the watermark to 60 seconds so all events are included, and accept the latency
options.why: Prioritises completeness over the stated 5-second requirement, which the stem rules out. It also penalises 100% of transactions with a 60-second delay to accommodate the 2% that are late.

options.text: Drop the late events and accept 2% inaccuracy, since fraud detection is probabilistic anyway
options.why: Simple and fast, but the late events are not a random sample — poor connectivity correlates with contexts that may matter, and systematically ignoring a segment is a poor property for a fraud system to have.

options.text: Process late events in a separate batch job that reconciles nightly
options.why: A legitimate lambda-style pattern that does eventually capture the data, and reconciliation has real value. But a fraud decision reconciled the next morning has missed its window entirely, so the correction arrives after it could act.

explanation: The instinct being tested is refusing a false dichotomy between latency and completeness by making results revisable. Emit at the deadline with what has arrived, mark the result provisional, and re-emit a corrected result when late events land within an allowed-lateness window. Fraud detection tolerates this naturally: a provisional 'allow' followed by a revised 'flag' is operationally fine, because the downstream action is review rather than an irreversible commitment. The costs are real and worth naming. Downstream consumers must be idempotent and keyed so a revision overwrites rather than duplicates, which means every sink needs an upsert path. State must be retained for the lateness window rather than discarded at window close, which is memory you have to size. And you need a clear contract about what 'provisional' means and how long revisions may arrive, because a consumer that treats the first result as final has reintroduced the bug. Two supporting design points. Set allowed lateness from measured arrival distributions rather than a guess — if 2% arrive within 60 seconds, look at what the 99.9th percentile actually is, because someone's phone will be offline for a week and you need a bound. And emit metrics on late-event volume and revision rate, since a rising revision rate is an early signal of an upstream problem and is otherwise invisible. The general principle: when a deadline and completeness conflict, ask whether the result can be corrected, because a revisable answer dissolves most such conflicts.
keyTakeaway: When latency and completeness conflict, make the result revisable: emit provisionally at the deadline and correct on late arrival — with idempotent sinks.

stem: A leader holds a 10-second lease and serves linearizable reads locally without contacting the quorum, on the grounds that it is still leader. NTP keeps clocks within 100ms. What must the design account for?

options.text: The lease must expire earlier by the maximum clock error, and the system must be safe when that bound is violated — an unbounded assumption becomes a correctness bug
options.why: Lease safety depends entirely on the leader believing the lease has expired no later than the followers do. NTP's typical accuracy is not a guarantee, so the design must subtract a skew margin and still behave correctly if skew exceeds it.

options.text: Local reads cannot be linearizable under any circumstances, so the optimisation must be abandoned
options.why: Overstated — lease reads are a standard, sound optimisation used in production systems including etcd and TiKV. They are safe given an explicit, enforced bound on clock error, which is what the design must supply.

options.text: The lease duration should be shortened to 1 second to reduce the window of risk
options.why: Shorter leases reduce exposure but raise renewal traffic, and the safety argument is unchanged — a skew larger than the margin breaks a 1-second lease as surely as a 10-second one. It trades cost for a smaller window without fixing the reasoning.

options.text: Reads should be served from followers instead, spreading the load and avoiding the leader's lease question
options.why: Follower reads are useful but need their own mechanism — read-index or a follower lease — to be linearizable, since a follower is by default behind. It relocates the problem rather than addressing the clock assumption.

explanation: Lease-based reads are how consensus systems avoid a quorum round trip on every read, and the safety argument is subtle. The leader may serve a read locally only if it is certain no other node could have become leader, which holds while its lease is valid. But 'valid' is judged by two parties with different clocks: the leader decides when its lease ends, and the followers decide when they may elect a successor. If the leader's clock runs slow relative to the followers', it can believe it still holds a lease that the followers consider expired — and then it serves a stale local read while a new leader is already accepting writes, breaking linearizability with no error anywhere. The remedy is to make the leader's view strictly more conservative: it treats the lease as ending earlier by the maximum assumed clock error, so it stops serving before any follower could act. That turns a timing assumption into an explicit, documented parameter. Two things must follow. The bound has to be enforced rather than assumed — monitor actual clock offset and have nodes step down when they cannot verify their own clock health, because NTP failures are common and silent. And the system should be designed so that violating the bound degrades rather than corrupts where possible: falling back to quorum reads under clock uncertainty costs latency instead of correctness. The general lesson is the transferable one — any correctness argument resting on a timing assumption needs that assumption written down, measured in production, and alerted on, because unmeasured assumptions are how systems fail in ways nobody can explain afterwards.
keyTakeaway: Lease reads are safe only with an explicit, enforced clock-skew margin. Write the timing assumption down, measure it, and alert when it breaks.

stem: An inventory service updates stock counts. Contention is low — 200 updates/second across 50,000 SKUs — but a handful of promotional SKUs receive thousands of concurrent updates during a flash sale. Which concurrency strategy fits?

options.text: Optimistic control for the general case, with a different mechanism for the hot SKUs — under heavy contention, optimistic retries collapse into wasted work
options.why: Two workloads with opposite contention profiles need different treatment. Optimistic concurrency is ideal at low contention and degrades badly at high contention, where most transactions abort and retry, burning capacity without progress.

options.text: Pessimistic locking everywhere, since correctness of stock counts is critical
options.why: Correctness is achievable with either approach; the difference is throughput. Locking every one of 50,000 low-contention SKUs pays lock acquisition and holding costs continuously to solve a problem that only exists for a handful of them.

options.text: Optimistic control everywhere, with an increased retry limit for the hot SKUs
